inline.s: The venerable Kong calculated that at fifty-three I would meet with disaster. I had never prayed for long life, and yet that year passed without the least harm; now I am sixty-nine. The Book says, “Heaven is hard to trust; the mandate is not constant,” and again, “The mandate is not forever fixed.” These are no deceiving words. From this I have come to understand that whenever calamity or fortune is spoken of, there is nothing that a person does not seek for himself; this is the word of the sages and worthies. To say that calamity and fortune are appointed by Heaven alone is the common talk of the world. What your own destiny will be, I cannot know. But even if your destiny should be honor and prominence, always think of yourself as forlorn; even if the times should run smoothly for you, always think of them as contrary; even if food enough lies before you, always think of yourself as poor and needy; even if others love and respect you, always think of yourself as one who should be afraid; even if your family's standing is high and weighty, always think of yourself as lowly; even if your learning is rather excellent, always think of yourself as shallow and crude. Think far ahead, how to spread abroad the virtue of your ancestors; think near at hand, how to cover over the faults of your parents. Think upward, how to repay the kindness of your country; think downward, how to build the blessing of your household. Think outward, how to relieve the urgent need of others; think inward, how to bar the door against your own wickedness. Day by day know your faults, day by day amend your errors. One day without knowing your faults is one day settled in self-approval; one day with no fault to amend is one day with no step to advance. There is no lack of clever and outstanding men in the world; the reason their virtue is not further cultivated and their work is not further broadened is only those two words, drifting along, which fritter away a whole life. The teaching on establishing one's destiny that Master Yungu imparted is a principle of the utmost refinement, the utmost depth, the utmost truth and the utmost uprightness. Savour it well and strive to put it into practice; do not let yourself idle away your days.

Good and evil are spoken of with respect to the human heart; retribution is spoken of with respect to heavenly principle. When the form is upright the shadow is upright; when the form is crooked the shadow is crooked. In every case the meaning is that not the least thing goes amiss. A good cause brings a joyful fruit; an evil cause brings a bitter fruit. The sages spoke of this in the greatest detail, yet foolish people will not believe it, and so they turn their backs on good and face toward evil. For they see that in the present age the good are sometimes beset by hardship and the wicked sometimes enjoy long life, and that what people receive in this world is of every kind and not uniform. So they claim that there are good and evil deeds that go unrewarded, and that cause and effect cannot quite be trusted. Do they not know that the world holds no one who lives several hundred years, and that Heaven has cases not yet closed? Those who are purely good or purely evil are few, while the pivot by which one may become good or evil is at its most supple. When a single thought turns, the retribution must be weighed accordingly. It may fall on oneself, or on one's children and grandchildren; it may fall in this present life, or in a later body. Great or small, soon or late, it shifts and changes, yet never misses by a hair. As the saying goes, “Good and evil at the last are always repaid; the only question is whether it comes early or late.” Do not judge by what lies before your eyes; look to the final outcome. How could it be anything but shadow following form? According to the Buddhist scriptures, there is a general teaching on the three periods of time: when sentient beings create karma, their retribution takes three forms. The first is retribution in this life, that is, receiving it in the present birth. The second is retribution in the next life, that is, receiving it in the second birth. The third is retribution in later lives, that is, receiving it in the third birth, and in the tenth, the hundredth, the thousandth, the ten-thousandth birth. Hence those in the world who do good and meet with calamity are ripening the evil of a former life; those who do evil and obtain fortune are ripening the good of a former life. Within fortune there is calamity and within calamity there is fortune, for no one is purely good or purely evil. Fortune at the start and calamity at the end means the good heart has retreated. Calamity at the start and fortune at the end means the evil heart has repented. When suffering and joy do not shift, that is open and direct retribution. When disaster and blessing alternate, that is hidden and subtle retribution. There are, further, hidden virtue and hidden fault, which are not the good and evil that people's ears and eyes can reach, nor are they retributions that people's ears and eyes can reach.

The extravagance of Luan Yan was repaid in his son; the death of Luan Ying was repaid in Luan Yan. Turned about and inverted, examples of this are many. As for Bai Qi burying the surrendered soldiers alive, and Li Linfu and Qin Hui spreading poison through the common people, their evil could not be exhausted in a single lifetime. In sum, the former life and the later life are one and the same life, and the punishment of men and the punishment of ghosts are one and the same pain; yet the world does not weigh this at all. How then has retribution ever gone astray? And yet someone will still say: a ruler rewards the good and punishes the wicked, and never prizes delay; why does Heaven not carry it out at once, so that people may be warned and afraid, instead of saying only that it lingers? Such a one does not know that the king's law still has its oversights, while the Way of Heaven has no such neglect; and that the ruler, unable to bear it, is sure to grant pardon and preserve, while the Mind of Heaven is utterly benevolent and ever permits one to repent of calamity. The ancients said that Heaven is the most patient of all; and in man there should likewise be an enduring heart. It is like owing a debt: the demand for repayment comes later, though the years allowed to each differ. One life, two lives, up to three, four, or five lives, are the great number that delimits Heaven and earth's repayment. When repayment is late, the interest is sure to be doubled; and what people see as long ages, Heaven sees as a single morning or evening. Therefore it is said: “In doing good and doing evil, retribution follows like a shadow. Do not say that the wicked go unrewarded; wait until their evil is brimming full. Do not say the good get no answer; wait until their good fruit is ripe and whole.” And again: “Though a hundred thousand kalpas pass, the karma one has made does not perish. When cause and condition come together, the fruit of retribution is still received by oneself.” From this we know that the suffering and joy of the three realms and the rising and sinking of the six paths are all summoned by one's own mind. The net of Heaven is hard to escape; if one tries to rush away and hide, it is like meeting rain on the road: whichever way one looks, all is soaked, and there is no place to dodge. Yet the people of the world do not awaken; they set it aside and do not examine it. Retributions that lie far off they of course never see; and even when they do see them, the ordinary run of good and bad turns they overlook without noticing. As for the credible cases of great good bringing blessing and great wickedness bringing disaster, they drag in other instances that have not been fully verified, and so dazzle and doubt themselves, sinking into hesitation and never turning back. Even if, after long experience, an awakening should suddenly arise, by then age has set their habits firm. And the young, whose bold spirit blazes, will not believe it either. This is why the world holds so many who have lost the road. How sad.

Huang Yongjue of Chongming in the Qing dynasty was judged by a physiognomist to be a man with no son at all, whose life would end at sixty. Later a ship from the southern seas was caught in a wind and about to capsize, and Huang quickly brought out ten ounces of silver, bought a fishing boat, and went to the rescue, saving thirteen lives. Meeting the physiognomist again, the man cried out in astonishment: “Your whole face is covered with the hidden-virtue lines. You must have done some great and generous deed. Not only will you have a son, he will come first in the metropolitan examination; and you yourself will reach a great age.” In the end he did have a son named Zhenfeng, who came first in the metropolitan examination in the jiwei year of the Kangxi reign; and he himself lived past ninety and died a good death. Such is the reliance that may be placed on the Way of Heaven. Why will people not forsake evil and do good?

Pan Qi, a butcher of Xiushui, did much that was unrighteous: he set people to quarrelling and litigating, seized others' goods and property, and violated other men's wives and daughters; and if the least thing went against his wishes, he cursed and reviled the gods and Heaven. Suddenly he died, and after a night came back to life. Calling his wife to gather the crowd, he said: “King Yama says that the dead receive retribution while the living do not know it; those who suffer are in agony, while those who commit the deeds still blaze away. This is truly pitiable and grievous. Now that Pan Qi's evil has reached its extreme, you are lent to him so that he may warn the ten thousand multitudes.” Then he took up a knife and cut off his own genitals, saying, “This is the retribution for spreading lust.” He gouged out his own eyes, saying, “This is the retribution for glaring with anger at immortals, buddhas, parents, and sentient beings.” He hacked off his own hands, saying, “This is the retribution for slaughtering living creatures.” He cut open his belly and carved out his heart, saying, “This is the retribution for secret malice and murderous cruelty.” He cut out his tongue, saying, “This is the retribution for deceit, falsehood, and cursing.” Far and near, people watched and spread the story, and none were not warned and afraid. Pan Qi lingered in agony for six days and died with no whole skin left on his body. He did it himself and suffered it himself, and so swiftly. The couplet at the Temple of Mount Tai reads: “In the world of the living the villain may harden his heart and injure principle — all of it his own doing; in the underworld the retribution comes — from ancient times to now, whom has it ever let pass?” Why will people knowingly offend and bring endless suffering on themselves? I pray that you rouse yourselves at once to warning and repentance, and each of you turn your head back early. Cleave the waves and ride the wind, but grip the helm firmly; rein in the horse at the cliff's edge, and pull hard on the bridle. Then all of you will leave the pass of calamity and together mount the road of blessing.

Cao Bin of the Song dynasty served his ruler with loyalty and honesty, and bore himself with modesty and respect. He was not eager for wealth or profit, and did not build up private obligations. He relieved the destitute and the cut off, and showed compassion to widowers and widows. Neither joy nor anger showed on his face, and in wealth and honour he was never arrogant. When he led armies on campaign he never put anyone to death wantonly. On taking Chengdu, when women had been taken captive, he shut them all in one room and passed food in to them through a hole, and warned those around him: “These are to be presented at court; guard them carefully and in secret.” When the affair was over, he sought out their families and returned them; those who had none he had married off with full ceremony. On taking Jinling, he first burned incense and swore before his troops that not one person should be killed without cause. Altogether, those he saved, before and after, were beyond counting. Other deeds of his: he set aside a grudge and cleared Chang Yan of blame; he took guilt upon himself to save Quan Bin; he delayed the execution of a newly married official; he would not harm insects already in hibernation. All were deeds of great virtue. His sons Wei, Cong, and Can in turn held the staff of command; his son Qi was enfeoffed as a prince; and the Empress Dowager Guangxian was born into the family. His descendants flourished beyond compare. Again, when Cao Han took Jiangzhou, he was enraged that the city had held out so long and slaughtered them all. When Cao Han died, not thirty years had passed before some of his descendants were beggars. Now the two generals' successes were one and the same, but their intentions were utterly different, and Heaven's recompense differed accordingly. To make one's posterity flourish greatly, the essential thing is to begin by setting one's own heart right. Sima Wengong said: “To pile up gold for one's descendants is no surety that they can keep it. To pile up books for one's descendants is no surety that they can read them. Better to pile up hidden virtue in the unseen dark, and one's descendants are certain to receive its recompense.”

Pan Congxian said: “A friend of mine, Ruan Jiantian, saw a butcher slaughter a pig whose hide bore the three characters Qin Bai Qi. This one is sunk in the ghost prison, and now and then is sent out in the body of some creature to make plain the retribution of karma. Over more than a thousand years, apart from the slaughter he suffers when reborn, the agony of the knife-mountain and sword-tree can never have ceased. Who knows in what year the Changping case will at last be closed. Again, a ploughing ox was struck dead by lightning. A scholar passing by said, ‘You do not strike down the evil in the world of men, but instead smite a ploughing ox in the field.’ No sooner had he spoken than the thunder struck the ox again, splitting its hide so that characters appeared, saying: ‘This is Li Linfu of the Tang dynasty. Three lives as a harlot, seven lives as an ox, and now it is finished.’ Reckoning from then to now, the retributions he received in rebirth in the world of the living amount to about three hundred years; beyond that, the severe punishments and extreme suffering of the underworld have scarcely known a single day's pause. And even to beg a brief turn as a harlot or an ox he could not obtain again. So hard is it for evil karma to escape the net of Heaven.”

This sentence down to “when the reckoning is exhausted, then death” forms one section. It says that in a person's one lifetime, through every day and night and every hour, and in every direction above and below and around, there are ghosts and spirits watching. In Heaven there are the Three Officials and the Five Emperors, the hundred spirits and their various bureaus; on earth there are the Five Peaks and Four Rivers, the City God and the local shrines. There is also the Bureau of Thought-Arising, which is charged with reporting the good and evil of people's rising thoughts. All these are the spirits who oversee faults. To offend means to summon it upon oneself. To seize means to take away. The reckoning is a hundred days.

The Mind of Heaven is benevolent and loving, and wishes people to do good and put away evil even in the place where they alone know. Therefore there are the spirits who oversee faults, who inspect what people have offended in, measure the weight of it, and seize their reckoning accordingly. Therefore it is said: “Private words among men sound like thunder to Heaven; a heart that fails in a dark room is seen by the gods' eyes as by lightning.” The Book of Songs and the Book of History likewise say: “God is upon you, and daily beholds you here”; “ten eyes see, ten hands point”; “the spirits hear it.” So in the place where my own heart alone knows, there are of itself ghosts and spirits, more stern than when all is displayed and arrayed in the open. This is the principle that Heaven and man are one.

The Avatamsaka Sutra says: “Each person's life has two heavenly beings who follow him: one is called Same-Birth, the other Same-Name. The heavenly beings constantly see the person; the person does not see the heavenly beings.” These are the two boy attendants of good and evil. In each day's twelve hours, wherever a person raises a thought, speaks a word, takes a step, meets a thing, or responds to a condition, he should constantly remember these two heavenly beings, and not let evil thoughts continue one after another. If by chance an evil thought should arise, he must quickly rouse his spirit and pull his head back around. To master oneself one must master the place hardest to master, and probe straight through to the place where thoughts arise and cease; then boundless karmic obstruction is in one moment made pure, limpid as empty space. If one does this, then the power to seize or to give lies with me, and ghosts and spirits cannot wield it. What need then to speak of spirits overseeing faults and seizing the reckoning?

Wang Yongyu of Yizhou in the Ming dynasty was a man of solid and generous character, sparing of speech, and had always honoured Lord Wenchang with the greatest care. He formed a society with his neighbours, and each New Year's Day they took turns building an altar and praying for blessing at the Wenchang palace on the summit of Yunzhong Mountain. In the society was a certain Yu Lin, famed for filial devotion and careful conduct, to whom people came from far and near carrying their book-boxes to study; and another, Yu Congzhou, of handsome figure and brilliant spirit, whose talk sparkled and who could dash off a thousand words at once. The neighbourhood gave way to these two. On New Year's Day of the xinyou year of the Zhengtong era, Yongyu went ahead to the palace and lodged at the altar, and dreamed that the Lord of Wenchang ascended his hall while the City Gods of the whole empire reported the rosters of the provincial examination. A spirit in court cap and crimson robe, holding a great ledger, came to present it for the Lord's signature. Yongyu secretly asked the ledger-bearing spirit: “In this province's roster, are there Wang Yongyu, Yu Lin, and Yu Congzhou?” The answer was: “No.” After a while, when the City Gods had withdrawn to wait, the crimson-robed spirit carried the ledger into the hall, knelt, and laid it before the desk. One by one the Lord read through it, writing a mark beneath each name; but there were some names at which he hesitated and did not set his brush. After a long time the crimson-robed spirit took up the ledger and proclaimed: “Return this to the City Gods of every province. Let them swiftly search out households of hidden virtue and sons of benevolence and generosity, and report their names to replace those in the roster left unmarked.” Yongyu hid himself under a pillar, and suddenly heard a summons from within the hall for Wang Yongyu to enter. He crawled up on his knees below the steps and was called forward to the desk. The Lord said: “Matters of rank and fame are secretly recorded by the celestial bureaus and may not lightly be disclosed. But because you have been utterly sincere, for more than ten years as if it were a single day, I have summoned you to explain them. Your grandfather was plain and careful, living by his own labour and never wronging anyone; he has already been entered for the provincial examination roster ahead of you, to make plain the recompense of a family's faithful generosity. But in all your life, when you met gods or buddhas you bowed your head and silently asked only that rank and fame go as you wished, and that your wife, the lady Yang, recover from her illness and that you grow old together. Though your widowed mother was living at home, you never prayed one word on her behalf. For this you have been set back two examinations, and you will pass in the fifty-third place on the lower roster. You should change your conduct, and no longer touch the Heart of Heaven.” Yongyu knocked his head and confessed his fault.

The Lord of Wenchang also said: “Zhou Ji of your society is the provincial examination's first-place graduate this year.” At that time Ji was the most timid and yielding of all the society, and his writing was not the equal of the others'; hearing this, Yongyu was utterly astonished and asked why Ji should take first place. The Lord said: “Zhou Ji's father and grandfather were both scholars, and never sent a single written word into a government office, and never violated a single woman. For three generations running they never once exposed a person's shortcoming or proclaimed a person's evil; and his great-grandfather composed a Discourse on the Hundred Endurances to exhort people, and many were moved and transformed by it. So for more than sixty years his father and son, grandfather and grandson, have laid the foundation of blessing in simplicity and quiet. This is hidden virtue of the highest order, and no one knows of it. The Supreme Emperor deeply approved, and entered prosperity for three generations; now that Ji has taken first place, it is only the first beginning of his blessing. Yongyu knocked his head again and said: “Yu Lin and Yu Congzhou of my society — may I ask whether they will pass?” The Lord examined the register of the scholars of Taiyuan, and his face seemed displeased. He said: “Yu Lin ought to take a degree; but because in serving his parents he murmured inwardly, and because he judges people with a biting harshness that comes near to inhumanity, while absurdly styling himself a noble man, his degree has been struck out, and he will be left to the end of his years frustrated among the common scholars.” Yongyu asked what was meant by murmuring inwardly. The Lord said: “Toward his parents, in his speech and bearing, his heart is always disapproving; he only forces himself to show nothing in his face or voice and drifts along complying with them. His true nature daily grows more remote, and he deals with them falsely — this is to look upon his parents as strangers. Feigning virtue to steal a name is what most provokes the anger of the gods; therefore he is punished.” As for Yu Congzhou, he was born with extraordinary talent: at twenty-six he would become a presented scholar, at thirty-odd he would be promoted to censor, at forty-five he would rise to Minister of Works and hold at once the seals of the offices of agriculture and justice, and at fifty-four he would retire as Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent, and at sixty-nine die a good death. But because from the age of seventeen, once he became a scholar, he relied on his talent and despised others, mocked and ridiculed and satirized, with words ever clever and cutting, the underworld bureaus have recorded more than two thousand four hundred and seventy entries of his frivolous verbal faults. The Supreme Emperor was shaken with anger, entered him in the register of hidden evil, and struck out all he had. If he does not repent, and the count passes three thousand, his span of life will be seized, and his descendants will be entered in the register of beggars. To wound the harmony of Heaven and earth and offend the taboo of the spirits — nothing is worse than this; therefore his offense ranks equal with killing living beings and with sexual misconduct. Be careful, all of you.” After a long while the Lord proclaimed again: “Of sexual misconduct, killing, and verbal faults, every thread and every grain is repaid; that need not be said. But of the two karmas of lust and killing, those who love themselves still know to keep the prohibitions. As for laughing and jeering with the mouth, mocking and satirizing at will, slaying in secret and thieving in the heart, one grows used to it and does not notice, until at last one's speech, looks, heart, and mind are entirely frivolous and slight; the ghosts and spirits record it all, and misfortune follows on one's heels. The blessings and endowments one was born with are suddenly changed into a poor and wretched husk. It is pitiable and fearful. You should broadly exhort the people of the world to take this as a warning, and spare me the great hesitation of signing the roster.” Yongyu bowed twice and withdrew. The morning bell startled him awake, and the cock had crowed three times. He bowed in thanks, took up his brush, and wrote it down. When the autumn roster was posted, Zhou Ji indeed stood first in the province. And so Yongyu spread this abroad to warn the world.

The Chan master Guangxiao An of the Song dynasty, in samadhi, saw two monks talking together. At first heavenly beings were guarding and protecting them and listening for a long while; then they dispersed. Presently evil ghosts spat and reviled them and swept away their footprints. It was because the two monks first discussed the Buddhadharma, then spoke of ordinary partings and reunions, and at the last talked of gain and support. Now if merely touching on worldly matters draws the anger and blame of ghosts and spirits, how much more so the deeds of body, speech, and mind of people today, which go far beyond this. How much heavier will the anger of the spirits and the blame of the ghosts be. This too is to be feared.

From here down to “when the reckoning is exhausted, then death,” all is a plain statement of the seizure of the reckoning. Poverty means having no wealth. Waste means the ruin of one's household. “Often meeting with” means that an unvirtuous person encounters these things everywhere. Sorrow arises from within himself; calamity is born from without. For the deceptions and concealments of an unvirtuous person are spied out by the spirits, so that his reckoning is reduced; hence poverty, waste, sorrow, and calamity come upon him heel to heel.

Fortune for the good and calamity for the lustful is the fixed principle of the creative order. If a person wishes to avoid the inauspicious and move toward the auspicious, he must turn to good and amend his faults. The essential thing is first to govern the mind and to examine his own three karmas, not letting them run loose and fall into the net of evil. One should exhort and warn one another in turn, mind and mouth instructing each other. The mind should say to the mouth: “You must speak what is good; do not speak what is unlawful.” And the mind should again say to the body: “You must walk in diligence; do not walk in idleness.” Day by day, hour by hour, moment by moment, thought by thought, down to a single instant, thus keep silence, mastering my own mind, guarding my own mouth, governing my own body. When this goes on long without interval, naturally the outer conditions will not stir the mind, and one is limpid and without desire, the whole being simply good. How then could one come to a reduced reckoning, to poverty and waste, sorrow and calamity?

Qian Ruoyu, magistrate of Fengfu, was crafty, dangerous, and secretly obstinate. In his early years he was appointed to office, but in many places he could not complete his term; in late life he grew even more distressed and obstructed, his sons and daughters perished, and he could not keep himself in food and clothing. So he prayed to the gods, and a god appeared to him in a dream and said: “Your offenses and evils have already cut down your reckoning to this. And still you complain of poverty and waste?”

Xu Xing of Wuzhong was greedy by nature and wicked. At first he was a broker in medicinal materials, and grew rich by extortion and cheating. Then, carrying his capital, he went to Liaodong to trade in ginseng, and there met with bandits and suffered the utmost terror, escaping by a hair from ten thousand deaths. Afterwards he went to Denglai in Shandong and again met an enemy who named him a remnant of the White Lotus sect and seized him to hand over to the authorities; he spent his whole fortune to escape. Last of all he went to Sichuan to trade in medicinal materials, and on the way back, when the boat was mid-journey, roving bandits suddenly appeared, and he abandoned his goods and came home. From then on his family declined, and he died of sorrow and depression.

To be hated means to be cast out and rejected. The Scripture of the Jade Pivot says: “If a person does not cultivate good karma, Heaven will surely cut off his spirit and take away his hun soul, so that he is turned upside down, hated by others, and harmed by others.” Now one who hates others for deceiving him does not know that Heaven has taken away his own mirror, so that he never meets with good times. If you have the good fortune to be alive today, you should ask to change your will and wash your heart, follow good and forsake evil; then the Mind of Heaven is benevolent and forgiving and does not put to death those who repent their offenses. Former faults may be redeemed and later conduct may be planned for. Whether one knows by birth or knows through hardship, success is the same. By no means give yourself up.

One who does evil is hated by everyone. This is because the common sense of right is in people, and because their true nature is fundamentally good. One should only hope to carry this single thought further: to see good and rush toward it as though one could never catch up, and to see what is not good as though drawing back from boiling water, and so urge oneself on into the ground where there is good and no evil. If one merely hates the evil in others without putting away the evil in oneself, how can one avoid being hated by others in turn?

Lai Junchen of the Tang dynasty was a censor; his bribes piled up like a mountain and the wronged dead choked the roads. At last he was executed in the marketplace for plotting treason, and people struggled to eat his flesh, gouging out his eyes and tearing out his heart, so that in a moment he was gone. Again, in the Song dynasty Ding Wei and Lord Kou Laigong were together in the government, and everyone in the empire spoke of Kou always as loyal and devoted, and of Ding always as treacherous and flattering. Hearing of one good deed, they always attributed it to Kou, though it was not necessarily Kou's doing; hearing of one evil deed, they always attributed it to Ding, though it was not necessarily Ding's doing. Again, in the Song dynasty Qin Hui deceived his ruler and ruined the state, and murdered the loyal and good. A hundred generations later, none do not hate his villainy; while King Yue's pure loyalty in serving the state is looked up to by all later ages. In his shrine there are iron statues of Qin Hui and his wife, Lady Wang, kneeling before the altar, and a wooden rod hangs there. People coming from far and near to pay their respects all bow reverently to King Yue, then take the wooden rod and beat the iron images. Put together, we see that the people have no private loves or private hatreds; what makes them differ is only the response to good and evil.

Punishment is the penalty of the officials; calamity is the affliction of Heaven. “Following” means keeping close and never leaving. The Perfected One of the Great Void said: “If a person brings calamity upon me, I send blessing in return; then the qi of blessing and virtue is ever born in me, while the qi of harm and heavy calamity is born of itself in him.” Here, when it says that punishment and calamity follow and settle upon the evil person, it means that the qi of harm and heavy calamity is constantly upon him.

The Avatamsaka Sutra says: “Within the continent of Jambudvipa, the sentient beings of the five turbidities do not cultivate the ten good deeds but devote themselves to evil karma: killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; false speech, idle speech, harsh speech, and divisive speech; greed, anger, and wrong views; they are unfilial to their parents and irreverent toward the Three Jewels; they contend with one another in anger and insult and defame one another, giving free rein to their feelings and opinions, and seeking what is unlawful. For these causes and conditions come weapons and famine, disease and death. Human calamity and heavenly punishment — in these various ways they receive retribution.” From this it appears that all is summoned by one's own karma and is not made by another. Yet turning aside or seeking a way out hinges on a single thought, and the hall of blessing and the prison of punishment lie right before one's eyes. If there were in truth a person who practiced all good and yet received evil retribution, that could never be so.

Liang Tong of the Han dynasty begged that the laws be made heavier. The court would not consent. Later a god appeared to Tong in a dream and said: “Though it is fortunate that the court did not follow your words, the underworld has already recorded your fault. You now wish to use punishments to injure others; can your descendants escape punishment? Having incurred guilt against Heaven, there is nowhere to pray.” All of Tong's sons died by violence, and when it came to Liang Ji, whose evil grew ever deeper, the clan was wiped out.

Wherever Liu Jia associated with anyone, calamity was sure to follow. Wang Jian did not believe it, and invited him to talk; before the day was out, Wang Jian's house caught fire. So he was nicknamed the owl, and all who saw him hurried away. Mei Cheng said: “Fortune is born with a foundation; calamity is born with a fetus. Take in the foundation, cut off the fetus, and from where can calamity come?” How true these words are.

To avoid means to seek and not obtain. The Way of Heaven has no favourites; it draws close only to the good. If a person can put away evil and do good, reverently governing himself and complying with Heaven, then naturally in stillness he joins with the Way, and in movement he meets with blessing. If he does the opposite, then in the open he suffers the penalties of the law, and in the hidden he lies under the execution of the spirits: his reckoning is seized, his life cut short, and the auspicious avoids him while the inauspicious follows. He cannot escape it.

Long ago there was a scholar named Wang, of a wicked and evil nature, whose every action went against principle and Heaven. He went to the autumn examination, and his essay was very good; the examining officer wished to recommend him for a high place. But when the roster was filled in, his paper suddenly could not be found; and when the filling was finished, the paper came out from the officer's own sleeve. The officer bitterly regretted it, met him secretly, and promised to make it up to him in some other matter. Before long the officer was transferred to the Ministry of Personnel, and the scholar at once paid in grain to enter the Imperial College; and when he went up for selection, the officer was serving in the office of selections, and was delighted to see him and secretly ordered that a fine vacancy be picked out and given to him by way of an extraordinary favour. When the time came, the officer had to withdraw from office because of his father's death. Three years later, when he was restored to office, he was again appointed to the office of selections; the scholar, too, by length of years, was due for selection and had a post assigned to him, and a fortune of ten thousand pieces of gold could be counted on. Within a few days, the scholar went into mourning for his mother's death. The officer, pitying his ill fate, recommended him to a provincial governor as a private tutor, from which three years might be expected to bring a thousand pieces of gold. Before a month had passed, the governor was removed from office over an old matter. Repeatedly he met with extraordinary opportunities, and every one turned to a painted cake. The scholar's resentment turned to sickness, and he lay abed for three years. Then one day he suddenly awakened and said: “It is all because my evil has piled up.” After that his illness gradually healed, and he did good for the rest of his life. Xue Xiyuan once said: “The blessings and emoluments within Heaven and earth will not gather to a person unless he keeps some heart of anxious diligence and vigilant effort; and they will not be dispelled from him unless he does nothing to help others and benefit creatures.” How true these words are.

The evil stars are the spirits who govern all calamities and disasters and hardships among men. A person living in the world belongs, day by day and season by season, to the governance of the star radiances. The heart of an evil person is constantly dark, and black qi rushes upward from him; by evil he summons evil, and so when the baleful luminaries draw near, they bring calamity upon him. But if he is a good person, his nature and substance are bright, and the evil atmosphere retreats and disperses; it will flee from him and fear it cannot flee fast enough — how much less would it bring him calamity? Alas, the evil is done by the person himself; the stars only bring calamity upon him. It is not the stars that bring the calamity; the person brings it on himself. It is not the stars that are evil; the person is evil himself. How then can a person fail to fear and examine himself, so as to turn back the will of Heaven?

Ma Zhangshi of Jucheng in Shandong relied on his talents and gave free rein to tyranny, stopping at no evil. One day a star fell upon his house and turned to stone. From then on lawsuits and quarrels, illnesses and the like, never ceased. A year later the magistrate died, his family scattered, and his house was left utterly empty. The stone, several feet around and faintly purple, bore markings like characters, and it is still there today.

This sentence is Taishang's earnest and repeated admonition. Sentient beings' evil habits are hard to uproot, and they commit every kind of unvirtuous deed; their vast karmic consciousness burns like fat in a fire, tormenting itself, losing day after day until the reckoning is seized to the last, and after death the guilt remains and they sink into the hells, into the realms of hungry ghosts and animals, into the three evil and perilous paths, where karmic retribution has no end and the wheel of suffering never stops. Who says that death settles everything and that there is no more to come? To speak of this is to be unable to keep from crying out aloud and weeping tears of blood. Alas, this human body is easily lost, and fixed karma — how shall one escape it? I can only hope that wise men and persons of resolve will believe deeply and without doubt, and while this single breath still remains, repent of evils that fill the sky. If instead they start and stop, drifting along, a hundred years will pass like an arrow, and when the four elements at last divide and scatter, will remorse be of any use?

Long ago an old man died and was brought before King Yama, and he blamed the king for not sending him word earlier. The king said: “Your eyes grew dim — that was the first message. Your ears grew deaf — that was the second. Your teeth were damaged — that was the third. All the members of your body declined day by day; the messages were beyond counting.” Then another man came, a youth, and he too blamed the king, saying: “My eyes are keen, my ears sharp, my teeth sound, and all my limbs strong and healthy. Why did you send me no message?” The king said: “A message was sent to you too. Do you not see that in the eastern neighbour's house some die at thirty or forty? In the western neighbour's some die at ten or twenty? And some die at a year old, or in infancy? All of these are messages.” Therefore it is said that human life is impermanent, compared to the morning dew; when one breath does not come, this body is only an empty shell. In the Sutra of Forty-Two Sections, the Buddha asked a monk: “How long is a human life?” He answered: “A few days.” The Buddha said: “You do not yet know the Way.” He asked another monk, who answered: “The space of a meal.” The Buddha said: “You do not yet know the Way.” He asked another monk, who answered: “The space of a breath.” The Buddha said: “Excellent. You know the Way.”

Chan master Tianru of Shizilin Temple in Gusu in the Yuan dynasty said: “The buddhas and patriarchs came into the world for one reason only: because each and every one of you has, right beneath your own feet, a great matter of birth and death, namely this, that you do not know where you came from when you were born, and do not know where you go when you die. This birth and death encompasses the whole great earth; from ancient times until now, not one person has escaped being swallowed by it. And do not speak only of ancient times; consider just since you were born, and think back ten or twenty years: how many relatives and friends have died? And do not speak of others; consider only yourself. This present four-element physical body you mistakenly take to be ‘I.’ From morning to night you cherish it in every way and nourish it in every way, yet it changes and decays thought by thought, gradually wasting away, and you do not perceive or know it. When the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, you will only find yourself all in confusion, like a crab dropped into boiling water. Where then are the heroes and great men of former days? And again, after death the bodily form and features change and decay, and the stench presses on people, so that even the closest flesh and blood will not consent to look straight at you. Where then are the affections and loyalties of a lifetime? Therefore the patriarchs said: ‘When one breath does not come, one is the same as dust and earth; the road ahead is vast and dark, and no one knows where one goes.’ To die and be burned just like that is pitiable enough in itself; how much more, when there is still the receiving of retribution according to karma. Here is where the crucial matter lies. What does it mean to receive retribution according to karma? Everything you have done in your life is karma; as soon as there is karma, there is retribution. Retribution follows karma as shadow follows form. When this body dies, the one consciousness-spirit may fall into the hells, or into the realms of hungry ghosts or animals, turning through rebirth and enduring immeasurable suffering. That is the realm where retribution is received. And what is the root of the karma of birth and death? That root is nothing but the single thought of this present moment. Since beginningless time, because of greed, anger, and delusion, because of ignorance and affliction, because of deluded thinking and the wild mind, you have met conditions and encountered circumstances, followed sounds and chased forms, and been thrown into seven kinds of confusion and eight kinds of inversion, so that there is no karma you have not made. This itself is the root of birth and death. When one thinks on the matter of birth and death, even an iron man's heart turns to ashes. Therefore the buddhas and patriarchs, bringing into play their vast compassion and pouring out their grief and pity, teach you to practice Chan and study the Way, and have you sweep away deluded thinking and the wild mind, recognize the master within, and know your original face. Then, while your eyes are bright and your legs still strong, you may become a pure and liberated person, and at the hour of death obtain great benefit, with birth and death no obstacle and going and staying both free. This is called finishing with birth and death and escaping it — a true great man indeed.”

Master Lianchi of Yunqi in Hangzhou in the Ming dynasty sang: “Do you not see the wife in the eastern house, strong as a tiger? She counted the months of her pregnancy still to come; last night she still leaned in her gateway, and this morning her fate has returned to the yellow earth. And do you not see the son in the western house, fierce as a dragon? At dusk he ate his fill and slept most deeply; his wandering soul went out and never came back, and by the fifth watch his life belonged to old Yama. People before your eyes are still like this; in distant places and other lands, who can count them? Search carefully through relatives and friends, and see how many have died as the years and months went by. Then you will believe the poet Ziyang: his words are true and indeed do not deceive. Yesterday he was still riding his horse in the street; today he lies a corpse in his coffin. Clever people, do not doze. Others are of the same kind as I; fox and hare look at each other, and there is not much to choose between them, yet how many examples lie right before your eyes. To drill into a horse's belly, to enter a cow's womb, and the heartbreak of the hells, are more pitiable still. If you would regain a human body, it is as slow as fishing a needle from the eastern sea — dawdle and you will be too late. I make this song, and it is truly bitter and keen; drop by drop the blood flows from my eyes. I earnestly exhort the people of the world to cultivate with all urgency; turn your head and wake at once, and you must decide for yourselves.”

Yan Bing of the Song dynasty, in his Essay Broadly Exhorting to Cultivation, said: “This physical body alone — who would believe that the body is the root of suffering? All crave the world's pleasures, not knowing that pleasure is the cause of suffering. This floating life is easily spent, and is no place for long dwelling; this phantom substance is not firm, and in the end comes to destruction. Before entering the womb, what male or female form was there? Only because earth, water, fire, and wind come together in a borrowed union does the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death, and of decay, become unavoidable. Above there is not a thread to hang it on; below there is no root from which it grows. Vain and floating, it is like a bubble on the water, gone in a moment; fragile and brittle, it is like dew on a blade of grass, vanished in an instant. Those of long life last no more than sixty or seventy years before all die; those of short life mostly die young at twenty or thirty. Some do not know today what tomorrow will bring; some are parted from the world between lying down and rising from bed. How many, when one breath does not come, are parted forever for a thousand autumns. Sigh that this body has nothing to commend it — yet who among men is not deceived by it? Sinews wrap a seven-foot frame of bone, skin wraps a bundle of flesh; from its nine openings impure things constantly flow, and through its six senses ignorance rages without restraint. Hair, down, nails, and teeth gather like heaped dust; snot, tears, and saliva are foul as a moving privy. Within, it is all a gathering-place of maggots; without, it draws clouds of mosquitoes and lice. Catch a single disaster or one disease and every one of them can kill a man; how much more the great heat and great cold, which hurry a person toward old age. The eyes are dragged by forms into the realm of hungry ghosts, the ears follow sounds into the Avichi hell. The mouth consumes a thousand flavours, and after death only a few drops of oil are added. This body deserves no love or pity; all of you should wish to escape from it. Why then do the deluded still put on airs of elegance, and the muddled still give rise to inversion? Some stick flowers and grass into a skull; some hang musk and incense at the side of a stinking skin bag. A gauze robe covers a bag of pus and blood; a brocade quilt hides a bucket of excrement and urine. They exhaust every scheming device of a treacherous heart, thinking to remain in the world ten thousand years, not knowing that when headache and blurred sight come, King Yama's messengers have already arrived; and when the hair at the temples is speckled and the teeth are damaged, the ghosts of impermanence send letters to seek one out. Every one of them clings to form and covets wealth — all of it a shortcut to losing the human body. Day by day they drink wine and eat meat — nothing but planting the deep root of hell. Before their eyes they snatch a moment's pleasure; behind them they will suffer bitter toil for ten thousand kalpas. Once the root of life is severed and the four elements are cut apart by the wind-blade, without, hands and feet are wrenched and drawn; within, liver and intestines ache and split.”

Even though wife and children cling to you in love, they have no means to keep you; even though flesh and blood fill the room before you, who will take your place? The living can only weep in bitter grief; the dead cannot escape their consciousness-spirit rushing wildly on. On the road ahead no light appears; lifting their eyes they find no companion at all. Crossing the river of no recourse, none who see it are not sorrowful; entering the ghost gate pass, all who arrive are desolate. In the world only seven days have passed, and in the underworld they are already hauled before the Ten Kings. The clerks of the bureaus hold the records and show no human feeling; the jailers hold their forks and have no smiling faces. Those who did good in life are sent back to the heavens, to the immortal paths, to the human path; those who did evil while alive are dragged into the paths of boiling water, of fire, and of blades. The cauldron of boiling water seethes as if a cliff were collapsing; the sword trees tower like mountains. Copper juice is poured in and the flesh of the whole body rots; iron pellets are swallowed and smoke rises from the whole mouth. Meeting with grinding and pounding, blood and flesh run down; entering the cold ice, the skin freezes and splits. The body is shattered and the karmic wind blows it back to life; when life ends the rakshasas shout and it lives again. Though one has passed through a hundred springs and autumns in the human world, in the prison only a single day and night have gone by. Though the hun and po souls have gone to the ghost realm, the corpse still lies in the coffin. Whether after three days or five, whether in the sixth month or the seventh, it rots and gives forth worms and blood, and its stench reaches the earth and the sky. Bloated and swollen, it is unbearable to look at; foul and hideous, it is truly dreadful. It is hurried off to a heap of wildfire, and buried in a waste of ten thousand miles of barren hills. The pretty rosy face of former days is turned to ashes; the desolate white bones of today become a heap of mud. All the love and affection of before comes to nothing here; the heroes of old — where are they now? When the rain of tears falls, all is empty and still; where the sorrowful wind moves, it is bleak and cold. At dead of night ghosts weep and spirits howl; as the years pass crows feed and sparrows peck. Beside the wild grass a stone tablet is left sprawling; among the green willows paper money hangs in vain. In the end none can escape this; when it comes to this, how can one not wake? Let everyone open their eyes, and no longer bury their heads. Turn the body about and leap out of the ford of delusion; snap the fingers and tear open the net of desire. Do not go on making a living in the den of ghosts. Know that within the lump of flesh there is a true person; whether man or woman, all can cultivate; whether wise or foolish, all have a share. Only turn the light around and shine it back, and you will know that the original substance was never there. If you cannot yet study the Way and practice Chan, then at least diligently keep the precepts and recite the Buddha's name. Forsake evil and return to good; change what is past and cultivate what is to come. Turn the six thieves into the six spiritual powers; leave the eight sufferings and gain the eight freedoms. Then you may well act as Heaven's deputy in transformation, and may freely receive people on the Buddha's behalf. Proclaim it to the crowd for the great assembly; explain it at home for the whole household. Make every place know awakening together; teach every person to escape sinking down. Above, aid the buddhas in turning the wheel of Dharma; below, pull sentient beings out of the sea of suffering. If you do not believe the Buddha's word, what word will you believe? If you do not cultivate the human path, the other paths are hard to cultivate. Do not let a single day pass and your skin be changed; though there be a thousand buddhas, they cannot save you then. Advance with all urgency; time waits for no one. Each of you, please take it up directly and do not let this life pass in vain.

This section says that in a person's single body, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, there are ghosts and spirits watching. The Three Terraces are six stars: the upper terrace governs destiny, the middle terrace governs blessing, and the lower terrace governs emolument; they preside over a person's life and death, his lifespan and early death. The Northern Dipper is the capital bureau of the purple pole, the origin of Heaven and earth, sun and moon, rivers, and seas, and it joins the virtues of yin and yang and of wood, fire, earth, metal, and water. It proclaims its majesty through the three realms, governs the ten thousand spirits, turns the cycles of qi, and weighs out death and life. When a person has offenses, they are entered in the register of evil, their weight is measured, and their reckoning is seized. A ji is twelve years. Again, Guan Lu said: “The Southern Dipper records birth, the Northern Dipper records death. When people receive the womb, all pass from the Southern Dipper to the Northern Dipper. If there is anything to pray for, one should face the Northern Dipper.” Again, the Seven Perfected Ones said: “On the third and the twenty-seventh day of every month I am sure to descend once to receive people's offerings and observe their good and evil.” Again, the Sutra of the Causes and Conditions of Karmic Retribution says: “The qi of the seven stars constantly gathers into a single star above a person's head, three inches above the crown. If the person does good, it is bright; if he does evil, its light is dim. With great good its light grows more brilliant; with great evil its light goes out. People do not see it, but ghosts and spirits do.” Here it says that above a person's head they record his offenses and seize his reckoning. Truly this is no falsehood.

Lou Shide of the Tang dynasty, in the reign of Emperor Gaozong, was laden with honours and favoured above others. One morning when he rose, a star official suddenly appeared to him and said: “You once killed two lives by mistake, and your offense requires the seizure of a ji. The light of your star is about to be exhausted.” That very day his spirit became confused; and he told people: “All my life I have been careful, and only because I killed two lives by mistake I shall now die one ji too early.” Before long he died as foretold. Zhang Gongchen said: “Lord Lou was long famed for clarity and forbearance, and was a weighty minister of the Tang; yet even he could not escape the seizure of a ji. How much less can ordinary people who do evil in a thousand ways? Must one not be careful?”

The present section teaches that the slightest stir of a person's mind is watched and examined by the spirits and gods. The upper corpse, Blue Maiden, is named Peng Ju and dwells in a person's head; she makes one full of thoughts and desires, dim of eye and falling of hair. The middle corpse, White Maiden, is named Peng Zhi and dwells in a person's intestines; she makes one greedy for food and forgetful, fond of doing evil deeds. The lower corpse, Blood Maiden, is named Peng Qiao and dwells in a person's feet; she makes one steeped in lust and fond of killing, so that limbs and organs are thrown into turmoil. The three corpses profit when a person dies quickly, for then they emerge and become ghosts, enjoying the offerings of blood and food. Therefore, on the day of gengshen, while a person lies asleep, they mount with the seven po souls of the body to the celestial bureaus, there to report that person's offenses. Of all the sayings that ghosts overhear from human mouths and minds, the three corpses are the foremost. People today do not know how to examine themselves and restrain themselves, to purify the mind and curb their desires; instead they put their trust in nothing but the Daoist practice of keeping watch on gengshen days and driving away the shen day, taking this as a way to cut off the three corpses' path of reporting. This only serves to deceive themselves. Do they not understand that if one's thoughts and deliberations are upright, the spirits and gods will of themselves withdraw, and what harm can the three corpses do? Master Cheng's poem for the night says: I do not keep the gengshen watch, nor do I doubt; this mind of mine forever leans upon the Way. Heaven above already knows how I walk and stand; let the Three Pengs say what they please.

The three corpses are simply the hun and po souls within a person's body. A person has three hun souls: the first is called Shuangling, the second Taiguang, the third Youjing. If an ordinary person calls their names aloud, the souls settle and the body finds peace. Again, the commentary to the Daode Jing says: the hun is the spirit of qi, and it has both pure and turbid; what the mouth and nose breathe is this, for the out-breath is yang extending and the in-breath is yin contracting. The po is the spirit of essence, and it has both empty and full; what the ears and eyes see and hear is this, for seeing is yang brightness and hearing is yin awareness. The yang spirit is the soul of the day, the yin spirit the po of the moon. Hence the realized person uses the hun to direct the po, while ordinary people use the po to capture the hun. By day the hun lodges in the eyes; by night the po hides in the liver. When the eyes do not look, the hun is in the liver; when the ears do not listen, the essence is in the kidneys; when the tongue does not stir, the spirit is in the heart; when the nose takes a single scent, the po is in the lungs. When these four leak nothing away, then the water of essence, the fire of spirit, the wood of the hun, and the metal of the po all gather within the earth of intention; this is called bringing the four families into harmony. Containing the light of the eyes, concentrating the resonance of the ears, regulating the breath of the nose, sealing the qi of the tongue, so that the four great elements do not stir and metal, wood, water, and fire all meet in the central palace, is called gathering and clustering the five phases. For because of the po there is essence, because of essence there is the hun, because of the hun there is spirit, because of spirit there is intention, and because of intention there is the po. These five run on without ceasing; and so this false mind of mine revolves through creation for countless myriads of years with no end. Therefore the sage, when the ten thousand things come, does not meet them with the mind but meets them with the nature. The nature is what is not yet stirred in the mind. Without mind there is no intention; without intention there is no hun; and so one is no longer subject to birth and death, and the round of rebirth comes to rest. The Perfected One Xu of Qiyan said: Always practice inner observation; dismiss the three corpses, drive out the six thieves, draw the qi into the cinnabar field, settle the mind in the ocean of enlightenment. When the mind is settled, the spirit is at peace and the qi abides; essence, qi, and spirit join, the three families walk together, and the holy embryo is formed. The Scripture of Clarity and Stillness says: The spirit of a person loves clarity, yet the mind disturbs it; the mind of a person loves stillness, yet desire drags it away. If one can constantly dismiss one's desires, the mind of itself grows still; if one clarifies the mind, the spirit of itself grows pure. Then naturally the six desires do not arise and the three poisons are wiped out. As for the Buddhist sutras, they say: With the sword of wisdom, destroy the thief of affliction. With the knife of wisdom, split the net of affliction. With the fire of wisdom, burn the fuel of affliction. Contemplate truly that the four great elements are fundamentally empty, and where can affliction plant its foot? Turn the three poisons into the three liberations, and turn affliction back into bodhi. In this way the three karmas become pure and the ten thousand virtues are complete, and what offense or evil remains to be spoken of?

The present section teaches that within a person's household, in every movement and rest, in every dwelling and place, there are spirits and gods who watch and examine. The dark of the moon is the last day of the lunar month. The Stove God is titled the Arbiter of Destinies, because he governs the fates of the noble and the lowly of a whole household. Morning and evening, no matter how slight the offense a person commits, there is nothing he does not examine; and at the month's end he reports it to the two luminaries of yin and yang, who record it in the black register. Alas! If the Stove God observes so clearly and holds such a charge of reporting, then when people of the world act, knowing only how to snatch pleasure for a moment, do they ever stop to ask whether the Stove God in their house has recorded their faults, and whether at each month's end the whole household's doings are reported to the celestial bureaus? Were they to fear this and examine themselves, not a single quarter of an hour could pass in slackness.

A scholar of Huai Commandery, drunk with wine, once made sport of a servant girl in his household. The girl had a fair sense of shame and firmly resisted until she got away. It was the last day of the first lunar month. He slept until the fourth watch, when his wife suddenly called him awake, saying, “Just now I saw a star, a spirit in black robes and cap, riding a horse and galloping along, with a register carried at his side. He pointed and gestured toward me as he went, and I do not know what he meant. The spirit's majesty was so awe-inspiring that I woke with a start.” The scholar's hair stood on end and his bones turned cold; he dared not say plainly what had happened, and said only, “It must surely have been the Stove God.” Afterwards, when the servant girl was given in marriage to another, he said to his wife, “The Stove God you dreamed of, who pointed and gestured toward you, came because I once made sport of this girl and she resisted with all her strength and escaped. I never expected that the same night would bring such a warning. I think that although the deed was not carried out, the intention had already betrayed Heaven, and so the Arbiter of Destinies recorded it. The reason I did not speak of it before was that I feared you would grow suspicious and that it would be hard on this girl. Now that I speak plainly, it is first to honour this girl's chastity, and second to expose my own fault.”

In the Jiajing era of the Ming dynasty there lived in Jiangxi a certain Mr. Yu, whose taboo name was Du and whose courtesy name was Liangchen. A man of many talents and wide learning, at eighteen he became a licensed scholar, and at every examination he placed in the highest rank. When he reached his prime his family was poor and he taught pupils. With more than ten fellow students of the same school he formed a Wenchang Society, cherishing written characters and setting living creatures free, abstaining from lust, killing, and faults of speech. He practiced this for several years. He sat for the examinations seven times, and never once passed. He had five sons; four died young of illness, and the third, a boy of unusual cleverness and comeliness who bore double moles on the sole of his left foot and was treasured by his parents, at the age of eight was playing in the village and was lost, no one knew where. He had four daughters, of whom only one survived. His wife, from weeping over her children, went blind in both eyes. Mr. Yu drifted through the years in failure, his poverty growing ever more bitter. He reflected that he had committed no great fault, yet he had wretchedly drawn down the punishment of Heaven. Past the age of forty, at the end of every twelfth lunar month he wrote out a yellow petition in his own hand and prayed before the Stove God, beseeching him to carry it up on high. Thus he did for several years, and there was still no response. When he reached the age of forty-seven, on New Year's Eve he sat through the night with his blind wife and his one daughter. The whole house was desolate, and they consoled one another in bleak sorrow. Suddenly he heard a knock at the door. Mr. Yu took up a candle and looked, and saw a scholar in a cloth cap and black robes, his beard and hair half grey, who bowed deeply and took a seat. He gave his surname as Zhang and said that he was returning from a long road, and having heard the sighs of sorrow from this house, had come especially to comfort them. Mr. Yu felt the man to be extraordinary, and treated him with the greatest courtesy. He then told of how all his life he had read books and accumulated good conduct, yet to this day had gained no official rank, his wife and children were not whole, and food and clothing did not follow one another. And he recited to Zhang the petitions to the Stove God that he had burned over the years. Zhang said, “I have long known of your family's affairs. Your evil intentions are far too heavy, and you devote yourself wholly to empty reputation. Every page is full of resentment and complaint, and you have rudely importuned the Most High; I fear the punishment you receive will not stop at this.” Mr. Yu was greatly startled and said, “I have heard that in the hidden realms the smallest good is certain to be recorded. I vowed to practice good deeds and have respectfully kept the rules for a long time. How can it all be empty reputation?” Zhang said, “Take for instance the article in your rules on cherishing written characters. Your pupils and your close friends often use old books and documents to paper windows and wrap things, and even to wipe tables, and they excuse themselves saying, ‘We must not let it be defiled,’ and then at once burn it. You see this with your own eyes day after day, yet you never utter a single word of warning. Only when you happen upon a scrap of written paper in the street do you pick it up and consign it to the fire: what good does that do? Each month the society released living creatures. You followed the crowd and ran along with them, letting others accomplish the deed; and if the others did not act, you too simply drifted. In truth the thought of compassion never stirred within you. And in your own kitchen, shrimp, crab, and the like were also served at table: were those alone not living beings? As for the article on faults of speech: your words are quick and brilliant, and those who talk with you are often carried away by you. When the words left your mouth, your own heart knew they wounded generosity. Yet in the familiar ease of talk among friends, you mocked and laughed along with every wind, and could not restrain yourself. Where the edge of your tongue reached, it angered and offended the spirits and gods. How many entries were written down as hidden evil, no one can count. And still you count yourself simple and generous. Whom do you deceive? Do you deceive Heaven? As for licentiousness, although there was no actual deed, whenever you saw another man's beautiful daughter or fair son you would stare long at them, and your mind would sway and could not be dismissed. It was only that no corrupt occasion happened to join with you. Reflect on yourself: if you were placed in such a situation, could you be like the man of Lu who turned away from the woman in the storm? To claim that in a whole lifetime you have done no licentious act, and that you can face Heaven, Earth, and the spirits and gods: that is truly false. This is how it stands even with the rules you vowed to keep, so what of all the rest? The petitions you burned year after year were all laid before Heaven. The Most High commanded the day-roaming envoys to examine your good and evil, and in several years not one genuine good deed could be recorded. Only in your private rooms and solitary places did they see your thoughts of greed, thoughts of lust, thoughts of envy, thoughts of petty impatience, thoughts of exalting yourself and belittling others, thoughts of brooding over the past and expecting the future, thoughts of repaying kindness and revenge. All these churned in your breast in numbers beyond counting. These various evil intentions, knotted tight within you, have been noted by the spirits in abundance, and Heaven's punishment grows heavier by the day. You have no leisure to escape calamity: how could you seek blessing?”

Mr. Yu was astonished, terrified, and trembling. He threw himself to the ground and said through his tears, “Since you understand the hidden affairs of the unseen, you must be a venerable spirit. I beg you to teach and save me.” Zhang said, “You have read books and understand propriety, and you also know how to delight in admiring the good. When you heard a good saying, you were stirred beyond measure; when you saw a good deed, you were elated beyond measure. But no sooner had the moment passed than you forgot it. The root of your faith was never deep, and so your constancy was not firm. Thus all your good words and good deeds over a lifetime were mere perfunctory drifting; not one thing was ever done solidly. And your breast was full of evil intentions, rising and falling, tangled and clinging, and still you wanted to demand fine reward from Heaven. It is like planting thorns over the whole land and foolishly hoping to reap fine grain. Is that not absurd? From this day forward, whenever thoughts of greed, lust, or puffed-up pride arise, or any delusive rambling notions, you must first summon fierce determination and sweep them all away, gathering yourself up perfectly clean. Let your single thought attend only to the side of good. As for good deeds that you have the strength to perform, seek no reward, court no fame, and regardless of size or difficulty, do them steadily and truly, with patience. As for those you have not the strength to perform, you must still, diligently and earnestly, bring that good intention to completeness. First you need a patient heart; second you need an enduring heart. Never grow lazy; never deceive yourself. Practice this long, and of itself there will come an unlooked-for proof. Your family has served me with much reverence and purity, and so I repay you with these words. Strive with all speed; the will of Heaven can be turned back.” When he had spoken, he went into Mr. Yu's inner chamber. Mr. Yu rose and followed him; when they reached the kitchen, he suddenly vanished. Then he understood that this was the Arbiter of Destinies, and he burned incense and bowed in thanks. On the very next day, the first of the new year, he bowed and prayed to Heaven and Earth, vowing to reform his former faults and to practice good deeds in earnest. He gave himself a new style, the Man of Pure Intent, vowing in his purpose to eliminate all delusion. On the first day of his practice, distracting thoughts came crowding in; if not doubt, then sloth. The days and hours slipped by, and he drifted as before. So before the image of Bodhisattva Guanyin enshrined in his family hall he bowed until his head bled, and reverently made a vow: may my good thoughts be true and pure, may my good effort advance with vigour; if I allow myself the least bit of self-indulgence, may I fall forever into the hells. Every morning at dawn he devoutly recited the holy name of the Great Compassionate One a hundred times, praying for hidden aid. From this time on, in every word and every action, in every thought and every moment, it was as though spirits and gods stood at his side, and he dared not deceive them or indulge himself. Whatever could benefit others or profit living things, no matter whether the matter was great or small, whether he was busy or at leisure, whether others knew of it or not, whether his strength could carry it through or not, he joyfully undertook and practiced it, bending every circumstance to accomplish it and only then stopping. Following conditions and finding what was expedient, he planted hidden merit far and wide. Moreover, with words of dutiful conduct, diligent study, humility, the patient endurance of insult, and the retribution of cause and effect, he taught and guided everyone he met, feeling each day too short. At the end of every month he would reckon up all that he had done and said in that month and write it out as a petition to report before the Stove God. Once he had held to this until it was ripe, in movement the ten thousand goods followed after him, and in stillness not a single thought arose. Thus for three years. In his fiftieth year, which was the jiaxu year, the second year of Wanli, he sat the metropolitan examination. Zhang Jiangling was chief minister. When the examination hall closed, Zhang inquired among his fellow townsmen, seeking a teacher for his son. Everyone with one voice recommended Mr. Yu, and so he was engaged and went to the capital. Mr. Yu brought his family with him. Zhang respected his virtue and character and had him admitted to the Imperial Academy by precedent. In the fourth year of Wanli, the bingzi year, he sat the provincial examination in the capital and passed; the next year he became a presented scholar. One day he paid a visit to the eunuch Yang, who had his five sons come out to bow. All of them Yang had sought out in every quarter to be his own heirs and to delight his old age. Among them was one boy of sixteen whose features Mr. Yu seemed to know well. He asked where the boy was from, and the boy said, “A man of Jiangyou. When I was small I strayed onto a grain boat. I still dimly remember my surname and my village.” Mr. Yu was greatly astonished, and bade him take off his left shoe. The double moles were there, unmistakable. Mr. Yu cried out, “This is my son!” Yang too was astounded, and at once gave the boy back, to return with Mr. Yu to his lodging. Mr. Yu ran to tell his wife. She clasped her son and wept bitterly, tears of blood bursting from her eyes; the boy wept too, and holding his mother's face in his hands, he licked her eyes, and his mother's sight was restored. Mr. Yu's grief and joy mingled. He no longer wished to hold office, took leave of Zhang Jiangling, and returned to his home district. Zhang, esteeming his sense of right, gave him generous gifts and sent him home. Living in his village, Mr. Yu practiced good with ever greater vigour. His son took a wife and in succession had seven sons, all of whom were raised, and all of whom continued the family's scholarly line. Mr. Yu wrote out with his own hand the story of his encounter with the Stove God and of his own honest practice of reforming his faults, to instruct his sons and grandsons. He himself enjoyed health and long life, reaching the age of eighty-eight. Everyone took it as proof that honest practice of good deeds can turn back the will of Heaven. Recorded by the later student of the same district, Luo Zhen.

The present section sums up the meaning of all that has gone before. It teaches that in a person's one lifetime, one body, one mind, and one household, there are spirits and gods everywhere, spread out in dense array. Therefore no fault, great or small, can ever escape their watching, and the reduction of years and the reduction of reckonings never miss by a hair. Whenever a person receives birth, his years and reckonings are all recorded in the heavens. The Most High commands the various spirits to examine and assess him: every three days one report, every ten days one memorial, every hundred days one reckoning. If he cultivates good and establishes merit, his years may be extended; but if by any chance he commits offense, the reduction and seizure come at once. Faults differ in greatness, and the years and reckonings taken away differ accordingly. The Most High does not shrink from painstaking words and repeated speech, expounding the principle that nothing is more visible than what is most hidden, all to teach people nothing more than vigilance in solitude.

In the Ming dynasty, the Great Master Wang Biru of Tiantai, whose taboo name was Ligu, received the provincial recommendation in the bingwu year of Wanli and was appointed magistrate of Xingan. In youth he had received the four precepts against killing, stealing, lust, and false speech, but later, because he held office, he let them lapse. In the wuwu year he went to court for audience, and his boat moored at Wuhu. He was seized and taken to the underworld, where he saw a king seated in a hall with two officials seated to either side. The king called his name and shouted at him, “Your life was due to end in the eighth month of the bingchen year. The reason you have been prolonged to this day is the power of your fasting and precepts. Why have you cast them away?” When he had spoken, he ordered a register brought to be shown to him. Under his name every year and month bore notations, but from the eighth month of bingchen onward it was blank. When the king had looked it over, Wang bowed his head and said in apology, “Holding office, the circumstances make it impossible to do otherwise.” The king said, “That is so. But what is to be done when your years in the world of the living are exhausted?” He ordered him driven into prison, and at once a ferocious ghost came, as if to seize and bind him. The official on the left petitioned, “Let us fetch the record of his deeds after he broke the precepts and examine it.” Presently two great chests were carried in, all containing the files of his administration at Xingan. Every note and every memorandum, even scraps of casually written paper an inch square, were all there, and from each a vapour rose, black, blue-black, crimson, or white, not all the same. He ordered each to be sorted into its own place. First the black and the blue-black were gathered together; next the white was gathered; next the crimson. The gathered blue-black pile faded from sight, and the black shrank to the size of a chopstick, while the crimson pile stood out brightly, alone and abundant. Wang, glancing sideways into that pile, saw that the Diamond Sutra and the Essay on Cherishing Life, which he had had printed, were both there. When the sorting was done, the master's voice softened somewhat, and he turned to the left-hand official and said, “So he knew how to plant virtue; he still has a way to live. Shall we damage his five senses and preserve his bodily life?” He ordered the prison guards to gouge out his eyes and set them on a pillar of the hall, where they shone brightly, casting light all around. Wang thought, “My eyes have been torn out; how can I still see?” At that very turn of thought everything suddenly went dark, and he could see neither hall nor officials nor guards. He only felt someone pat his back, saying, “Go quickly, go quickly.” After a moment he stumbled and woke. The next day both his eyes went blind. He then abandoned his household and cultivated the Way. Later, through Chan awakening, his sight returned. He travelled widely among the communities of Yunqi and Boshan, truly investigating and truly realizing, and also practiced the Great Compassion Repentance.
