He lived twelve years after being born again. Now a person, apart from sages and worthies, never passes a day without being in the midst of faults. The only thing he can rely on to turn back creation is the ability to reform. Otherwise, his former causes being already poor, his later karma only increases; and even with abundant fortune and many sons, when the moment comes that the last breath does not return, nothing goes with him but his karma. He sees only the bitterness of King Yama's reckoning. Can his property be carried away? Can his sons and daughters take his place? Think on this, think on this.

In the Song dynasty, Fu Zhongxin was rich and loved to give. At the age of thirty-five he suddenly fell gravely ill. He said that he had gone to the underworld and there met several old acquaintances, who called out, “Benefactor, what brings you here?” Together they bowed and pleaded with a clerk. The clerk said, “This man was originally destined for hunger and cold, but because his heart loved to give relief, he was able to rise from nothing to a prosperous house. His lifespan was originally fifty-nine years, but because he did not burn incense and rose late from sleep, all of it has now been cut away.” The several men said, “These two are small faults. How can they come to this?” The clerk said, “Not burning incense means having no heart to revere Heaven and Earth. Rising late from sleep means harbouring thoughts of lust. How are these small faults?” The crowd looked at one another in astonishment and said, “Even a man of such deep virtue as Mr. Fu is cut down for this. Can anyone then give himself free rein?” Before long he died. Now the most difficult thing for a person to obtain is long life, and it is also long life that is seized away in the underworld. Therefore the Most High speaks of this earnestly and repeatedly, to warn people to be careful of a single mistaken thought, so that they may be first in enjoying the five blessings. Herein is the Most High's compassion at its greatest.

The several hundred matters begin with acting contrary to right and end with reaching even to death. Earlier the text spoke of reduction and seizure, teaching people to know what to guard against. Here it speaks of long life, teaching people to know what to aspire to. The phrase “one must first avoid” does not mean that others need not avoid them; it means that those who wish to seek long life should guard against them with special care, so that not even a thread of silk or a speck of dust clouding the eye is allowed to remain.

For the student of the Way, planting virtue is the root. In Confucianism it is the four beginnings and the hundred practices; in Buddhism the six perfections and the ten thousand practices; in Daoism the three thousand merits and eight hundred practices. All are teachings of accumulating good and avoiding evil. Yet if one wishes to accumulate good and reform faults, nothing comes before realizing the ultimate Way; and if one wishes to realize the ultimate Way, nothing compares to clarifying one's original mind. The mind is the substance of the Way; the Way is the function of the mind. If a person can observe the mind and contemplate the nature, then the perfect and luminous substance appears of itself, and the function of non-doing is accomplished of itself. Without resort to effort he leaps beyond the far shore. Were the mirror of the mind not bright and clear, the divine pearl not vast and translucent, how could he cause all appearances to fall away at once, not a hair's breadth defiled, the source of mind wholly free, and decisively attain the unborn? Therefore the person who clarifies the mind and realizes the Way does not let the body burden his nature or circumstances disorder his truth. In responding to conditions and meeting things, he lodges within himself the meaning of the unborn. This is what is called the supreme, most true, and wondrous Way.

The female immortal Yang Zhengjian was on the very day of her ascension to the ranks of the perfected, when the Most High censured her for something from her youth. Her father and mother had been stringing coins to pay their taxes, and Zhengjian, against propriety, had picked out two coins that were round and fine and hidden them away. This was called concealing official property, and she was further banished to remain in the human world for one more year. The Primordial Lady of Purple Emptiness and Lord Mao were together in the Palace of Pure Emptiness, examining the gains and losses of all the perfected immortals under Heaven. Those who fell at once numbered forty-seven, while those who rose again were only two. This was because harbouring a heart of lust while performing the work of the highest truth cannot be without fault. Now hiding a coin is a small fault, and these immortals were ones whose merit and fault balanced each other, yet they were still censured like this; how much more those who follow their inclinations without avoidance? Those today who seek long life trust only in storing essence and holding the breath, refining medicines and burning cinnabar, and then say that the true immortals may be met. They do not know that all of this is outside the Way. Only cultivating truth and refining the nature, so that every deluded thought is noticed the instant it sprouts and extinguished the instant it is noticed, striving to keep the twelve double-hours pure as a bright pearl, with the mind at peace and empty, so that the Way comes of itself to dwell there, brings lengthened years and increased lifespan by a principle that is simply so.

In the Ming dynasty Yuan Liaofan's chapter on reforming faults says: When the great officers of the Spring and Autumn period heard a person's words and observed his actions, they would infer and foretell his calamity or fortune, and there was none whose words failed to come true; the records in the Zuo Commentary and the Guoyu may be consulted. In general, the omens of good and ill fortune sprout in the mind and then stir in the four limbs. Those whose conduct leans to generosity often obtain blessing; those whose conduct leans to meanness often draw near calamity. The worldly eye is mostly clouded, and people say that fortune and calamity are undetermined and unfathomable. But utmost sincerity joins with Heaven: when fortune is about to arrive, one observes the person's good and is sure to know it beforehand; when calamity is about to arrive, one observes his evil and is sure to know it beforehand. Now if one wishes to obtain fortune and keep calamity far off, before speaking of doing good one must first reform one's faults. As for one who reforms faults, first he must rouse a heart of shame. Let him think: the sages and worthies of old were men like me, and I am a man like them. Why is it that they can be teachers for a hundred generations, while I am shattered like a broken tile? Because I am steeped and stained in worldly feeling and secretly do what is unrighteous, saying that others do not know, proud and unashamed, so that day by day I sink toward the birds and beasts without knowing it. Of all things in the world that are shameful and disgraceful, nothing is greater than this. Mencius said, “Shame is of the greatest importance to a person: by gaining it one becomes a sage or a worthy; by losing it one becomes a bird or a beast.” This is the crucial pivot of reforming faults. Second, he must rouse a heart of fear. Heaven and Earth are above us, and the spirits and gods are hard to deceive. Though my fault lies hidden and subtle, Heaven, Earth, and the spirits and gods truly observe it from on high: in heavy cases they send down a hundred calamities, in light cases they diminish my present blessings. How can I not be afraid? Nor is this all. In a place of quiet retirement, pointing fingers and watching eyes are perfectly plain. Though I cover a thing very closely and gloss it very cleverly, my lungs and liver are already exposed, and in the end it is hard to deceive myself. Once another sees through it, it is worth less than a penny. Can I fail to tremble? Nor is this all. So long as a single breath remains, even Heaven-filling evil can still be repented and reformed. The ancients had men who did evil all their lives and, at the point of death, repented and awoke, rousing one good thought, and so obtained a good end. It is said that one thought of fierce resolve is enough to wash away a hundred years of evil. It is like a valley dark for a thousand years: let a single lamp shine, and the darkness of a thousand years is wholly dispelled. Therefore a fault is not judged by whether it is old or recent; what is valued is only the reforming of it. But this dusty world is impermanent, and the physical body is easily lost. When the last breath no longer belongs to me, there will be no way to reform. In the visible world, for a thousand or a hundred years I bear an evil name, and even filial sons and loving grandsons cannot wash it away. In the hidden world, for a hundred or a thousand kalpas I sink into the retribution of the hells, and even sages, worthies, Buddhas, and bodhisattvas cannot draw me out. How then can I not fear? Third, he must rouse a heart of courage. When people do not reform their faults, it is mostly because they drift along and shrink back. I must rouse myself with vigour, without hesitation, without waiting. A small fault is like a thorn in the flesh: pull it out at once. A great fault is like a poisonous snake biting the finger: cut it off at once. Not the slightest hesitation may remain. This is why the wind and thunder of the Yi Jing make up the hexagram of increase.

With these three hearts complete, faults are reformed as soon as they appear, like spring ice meeting the sun: what fear is there that they will not melt? Yet a person's faults may be reformed from the level of action, from the level of principle, or from the level of mind; the work differs, and the proof differs as well. If previously one killed living beings and now one refrains from killing, or previously one raged and cursed and now one refrains from anger, this is reforming at the level of the action. To force restraint from outside is a hundred times harder, and the root of the disease remains: it dies in the east and is born in the west. This is not the way of final and complete clearing. One who is good at reforming faults, before prohibiting the act, first clarifies the principle. Suppose the fault lies in killing living beings. Then one thinks: the Most High loves life, and every creature clings to its life. To kill another to nourish myself, how can I be at peace? And when that creature is killed, it suffers slaughter and cutting and then is put into the cauldron, its various pains piercing to the marrow. As for my own nourishment, when rich meats and fine delicacies are spread out, they are gone as soon as they are eaten, while vegetables and soups can perfectly fill the belly. Why then must I destroy another's life and diminish my own blessing? Again one thinks: all beings that have blood and breath contain a spiritual awareness. Since that spiritual awareness is mine, they are all one body with me. Even if I cannot personally cultivate the highest virtue and make them honour and love me, how can I day after day destroy living creatures and make them hate and resent me without end? Once this thought is reached, there will be those who grieve over their food and cannot swallow it. Suppose again that previously one was fond of anger. One must think: where people fall short, their circumstances deserve pity. If they oppose me against reason, what has that to do with me? There is in truth nothing to be angry about. Again one thinks: in all the world there is no hero who is always right, nor any learning that blames others. Whenever action fails to obtain its end, it is always because my own virtue is uncultivated and my influence has not reached. If I turn everything back upon myself, then when slander and abuse come, they all become ground for polishing and perfecting me, and I will gladly accept them as a gift. What anger can there be? Again, if one hears slander and is not angry, then though the flames of calumny smoke to the heavens, it is like lifting a torch to burn the empty sky: in the end it will die down of itself. If one hears slander and is angry, then though one strive with a clever mind to argue it away, it is like a spring silkworm making its cocoon, binding itself. Anger is not only useless; it is also harmful. All the other kinds of faults and evils should likewise be considered in the light of principle. Once the principle is clear, the fault will stop of itself.

What does it mean to reform from the mind? Faults have a thousand forms, but they are all made by the mind. If my mind does not stir, how can faults arise? For the student, in regard to lust, fame, goods, and anger, and all the various offenses, there is no need to seek them out one category at a time. He need only set his whole mind on good, so that right mindfulness stands before him at every moment, and then evil thoughts of themselves cannot defile him, like the sun standing in the empty sky, before which the spectres of the dark silently dissolve. This is the true transmission of singleness and purity. Faults are made by the mind and are also reformed by the mind. It is like cutting down a poisonous tree: cut straight through its root; why must one hack at every branch and pluck every leaf? In general, the highest way is to govern the mind, and at once there is purity. As soon as a thought stirs, one notices it; and having noticed it, it is gone. If one cannot yet do this, one must clarify the principle to dismiss it; if one still cannot, one must prohibit it deed by deed. To undertake the higher matter while also practicing the lower work is not a poor plan; but to cling to the lower and be blind to the higher is clumsy. Moreover, when one makes the vow to reform faults, in the visible world one needs good friends to remind one, and in the hidden world one needs the spirits and gods to bear witness. With a single mind one repents, without slackening day or night, for one seven-day period, two seven-day periods, and on to one, two, or three months, and there is certain to be proof. Perhaps one feels the mind at ease and expansive; perhaps one feels wisdom suddenly open; perhaps in the midst of tangled affairs every thought one touches becomes clear; perhaps meeting an enemy one turns wrath into joy; perhaps one dreams of spitting out black things; perhaps one dreams of sages and worthies of old reaching down to lift and guide one; perhaps one dreams of flying through the empty sky; perhaps one dreams of banners and jewelled canopies. All such excellent things are signs that faults are dissolved and offenses wiped away. Yet one must not cling to them and exalt oneself, drawing a line and going no further. Long ago Qu Boyu, at the age of twenty, already perceived the wrongs of former days and reformed them all. At twenty-one he realized that what he had reformed before was not yet complete. At twenty-two, looking back on twenty-one, it was like a dream. Year after year he reformed one layer after another, and at the age of fifty he still knew the wrongs of his forty-nine years. Such was the learning of the ancients in reforming faults. We who are ordinary people have faults and evils piled up like a hedgehog's quills, yet when we look back on past affairs we often do not see that we had any faults at all: our minds are coarse and our eyes clouded. Yet those whose faults and evils are deep and heavy also have their proofs: perhaps the mind and spirit grow dull and blocked, so that one forgets a thing the moment one turns one's head; perhaps one is constantly vexed for no reason; perhaps in the presence of a noble person one flushes with shame and wilts; perhaps on hearing right discourse one is displeased; perhaps one shows kindness and others resent it instead; perhaps one's dreams at night are topsy-turvy; and in extreme cases one speaks wildly and loses one's resolve. All these are marks of having made karma. If any one of them fits, one must rouse oneself and strive, forsake the old and seek the new, and take care not to ruin oneself.

From this point down to the three hundred good deeds, the text truly speaks of the works of doing good, by which a person who embodies and practices them at once obtains the reward of blessing. The Way is like a great road: to follow heavenly principle and accord with the human heart, level, plain, upright, and straight, is the Way; to go against heavenly principle and offend the human heart, through thorns and perilous steeps, is not the Way. These two lines belong, the one to turning toward good, the other to reforming faults; yet they are one single intent, for to withdraw from what is not the Way and advance into this Way comes down to nothing but one good. The two words “then” are the place to grip hard and put forth strength. Right and wrong must be discerned in the present thought, and advance or retreat decided on the instant. Here one must use the method of the knife that cuts nails and severs iron, with no room for the least delay. Turn the thought aside and one falls back into the demon's gate; therefore one must examine oneself at every moment and cultivate carefully in every matter, and only then does one grasp this meaning.

This Way is the Way of which it is said, what Heaven decrees is called the nature, and to follow the nature is called the Way. In the course of daily use, in speech and silence, in movement and stillness, there is no place where it is not. One need only know it truly and practice it bravely. An ancient worthy said, “The great Way does not depart from what is before your eyes; and yet what is before your eyes is hard to see. If you would know the true substance of the great Way, it does not depart from sound, form, speech, and words.” The Daode Jing says, “When the highest type of person hears the Way, he practices it diligently.” The Neiguan Jing says, “To know the Way is easy; to have faith in the Way is hard. To have faith in the Way is easy; to practice the Way is hard.” The Avatamsaka Sutra says, “Faith is the mother of the source of the Way and of all merit; it nurtures and sustains all roots of goodness. It cuts off the net of doubt and brings one out of the river of craving, revealing the supreme Way of nirvana.” For the substance of the Way is complete in every person. Even amid the drowning of ten thousand desires, if one is willing to turn the light back for a single thought, what is true and what is false will of themselves not be concealed by so much as a hair, and this is what is called the substance of heavenly principle that never ceases. Extend it and fill it out, and through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lives one will not fall into degradation. When knowledge and practice are one, entering sagehood is not difficult. How true this is!

Long ago there was a farmer who had once been mauled by a tiger. When someone spoke of a tiger mauling a person, everyone was startled, but the farmer alone turned strangely pale. Now that a tiger can maul a person, there is no one who does not know it; yet because they have not experienced it themselves, they only startle for a moment. The farmer had suffered the pain in his own body, and so his colour changed. When people know that a thing is not the Way and yet still do it, it is likewise because they have not truly known. If they truly knew, they would never do it. People today pass day and night in a daze, like men talking in their sleep. Only by keeping the breath alive in each instant, so that this mind is alert and clear, one point of spiritual light forever still and forever shining, does the original substance remain free even as worldly conditions rise and fall around it. Only this is the Way that is known alike through the day and through the night, and nothing that is not the Way can confuse or disorder such a one.

In the Song dynasty, Lord Zhao Qingxian every night burned incense and reported to Heaven. Someone asked him about it, and he said, “From my youth up, whatever I have done by day I must at night bow and report to the Most High. What I dare not report, I dare not do.”

Zhang Qiyun devoted himself to the study of the nature and principle, and set his resolve firmly on filial piety and brotherly love. In every word and every action he moved in accord with propriety and law. At the slightest mistake he would reproach himself bitterly, repent, and reform, and would lie awake the whole night. After his father and mother died, whenever he met with the foods they had loved in life, he would always bow his head over them and weep. Husband and wife revered one another as though they were guests, and to the end of his life he had no second woman. His household was kept strict and grave; even at leisure and alone he never wore a slovenly look. When he saw the younger members of the family, he was sure to exhort them diligently, so that they might succeed. When his kin and friends met with urgent trouble and his own strength could not cover it, he would seek aid in every quarter, begging and petitioning to rescue them; when the matter succeeded he was glad, and when it did not he sighed in sorrow without ceasing. In his later years he advanced still more diligently. He often said, “From my great-great-grandfather Lord Guanxin, my family has laid its foundation in filial piety and brotherly love, and generation after generation has kept to loyalty and generosity. My nature is simple, and I cannot manage property to leave to my sons and grandsons. I ask only that I not disgrace the family name, but preserve this one field of the heart and leave it for those who come after me to till.”

In the Later Han, Guan Ning once dug in the ground with Hua Xin and found gold. Ning did not look at it; Xin picked it up and threw it away. When the world fell into disorder, Ning took refuge in Liaodong. Gongsun Du treated him with courtesy, but he would not take office. He made his dwelling among the hills, and many people followed him. When a neighbour's ox trampled his field, Ning led it to a waste place and pastured it there, and the ox's owner, ashamed, came to apologize. The place where he lived gradually grew into a settlement. There Ning expounded the Book of Songs and the Book of Documents, set out the sacrificial vessels, and made clear propriety and yielding. Anyone who was not a student of learning never came before him. His influence spread through Liaodong, and the people were transformed by his virtue. Whenever he saw Gongsun Du, he spoke only of the Way and virtue, never touching worldly affairs, and Du was content with his worth. After thirty-seven years in Liaodong he returned by sea at an imperial summons. A great gale arose and the waves ran high, and the boatmen cried out to Heaven, confessing their sins. Ning said, “Once I went bareheaded for a whole morning, three mornings I rose late, and once I went to the privy without my cap. My fault must lie in these.” All the other boats travelling with them were lost; only Ning's boat came through. On his return he was offered the post of Grand Master of the Palace, which he did not accept. Hua Xin wished to yield the post of Grand Commandant to him, and he declined that as well. He died at the age of eighty-four. The wooden couch he sat on was worn through where his knees rested, because for fifty years he had never once sat with his legs spread out. When kinsmen or neighbours were poor and their households could not hold so much as a picul of grain, he was sure to divide his own and relieve them. To sons he spoke of filial piety, to younger brothers of fraternal duty, to officials of loyalty. In appearance reverent and in speech compliant, he could use every occasion to guide people toward good, and no one who felt shame failed to be transformed. Now let people today consider: in the course of the day and night, when family members cross their wishes, do they give rise to vexation? Living at ease, warm and well fed, do they give rise to lust? When their livelihood is thin, do they give rise to schemes for profit? When companions on the Way are parted and scattered, do they give rise to dullness and sloth? When their attachment to home weighs heavy, do they not think longingly of fields and houses? Seeing others rich and honoured, do they not think of glory? Being themselves poor and lowly, do they not think of scrambling after advancement? If any one of these is present, it is enough to turn back the mind of the Way and make one enter what is contrary to reason. This must not be taken lightly. Therefore examining oneself is the substance of learning, and knowing one's faults is the advance of the Way.

To tread means what the body walks upon and what the thought reaches, both alike. A byway means what is exceedingly subtle and easily overlooked, namely the crookedness of a single act or a single thought. To deceive means to offend knowingly; the dark room is the place where no one sees and no one hears, the border where good and evil first divide. Not to tread byways means that from the very source of the mind one has arranged things squarely and uprightly, so that though a crooked path be a thing of the smallest consequence, at this point one decisively will not walk it; and then one may know what one will do in greater matters. Not to deceive in the dark room means that from the very source of the mind one has swept things perfectly bright and clear, so that though it be a matter known to oneself alone in the corner of a leaking room, its working utterly hidden, at this point one decisively will not be careless; and then one may know what one will do in the open. Only when one can be like this does the accumulating of virtue and the piling up of merit, and all the various good deeds, hang together as one.

Blessing is the reward of virtue. The moment there is the least thought of seeking it, that is already a byway. Therefore one should create blessing for one's sons and grandsons, not seek blessing for them. To keep the family rules strict, to prize frugality and simplicity, to teach farming and letters, to accumulate hidden virtue: this is to create blessing. To widen fields and houses, to forge marriage alliances, to wrangle over a tenth share, to traffic in official rank: this is to seek blessing. The one who creates blessing is mild and long-enduring; the one who seeks blessing is rank and short-lived. Reputation is the guest of reality. The moment there is the least thought of selling it, that is already a byway. Therefore one should cherish one's name for this life, not market it. To give weight to poetry and letters, to honour spirit and integrity, to be careful in what one takes and gives, to guard one's dignified bearing: this is to cherish one's name. To vie in advertising oneself, to court the powerful and noble, to chase after the ostentatious and extreme, to practise ambiguity: this is to market one's name. The one who cherishes his name is quiet and at rest; the one who markets his name is restless and clumsy. Wealth is for nourishing life. The moment there is the least thought of squandering it, that is already a byway. Therefore one should use one's wealth for the family, not squander it for the family. To relieve one's clan, to broaden the fees one pays for teaching, to save against famine and be sparing, to assist righteous undertakings: this is to use wealth. To lavish palaces and gardens, to keep singers and dancers, to be extravagant in banquets, to gather treasures and curios: this is to squander wealth. The one who uses wealth loses and yet is full; the one who squanders wealth is replete and yet empty. As the head of a family, the moment there is the least thought of self-interest, that is already a byway. Therefore one should cultivate oneself for the sake of all under Heaven, not keep oneself for the sake of all under Heaven. To reduce one's appetites and desires, to lessen one's thoughts and cares, to guard against anger and wrath, to moderate food and drink: this is to cultivate oneself. To scheme for advantage and harm, to shun toil and resentment, to build oneself a den, to hold fast to wife and children: this is to keep oneself. The one who cultivates himself is sparing and yet great; the one who keeps himself is rank-smelling and small.

The Perfected Lord Yisheng admonished Zhang Shouzhen, saying, “If you can discipline yourself and hold to uprightness, so as not to deceive your own heart, you will of yourself silently accord with heavenly principle.” Lord Guan, the Emperor Sage, said, “A person has a mind as Heaven has the sun: its light shines through and illuminates, revealing every detail without partiality.” Lu Xiangshan said, “A person has but one mind, and when it stirs it becomes thought and deliberation. Whether the thought is upright or not lies only in an instant. If a single thought is not upright, and one knows it in that instant, then one can set it right; if an upright thought is lost in an instant, then it has become not upright. All of this lies within a person's one mind.” The Book of Documents says, “Without mindfulness even a sage may become a madman; through mindfulness even a madman may become a sage.” Through a thousand ages the sages and worthies did nothing more than examine the subtlety of a single thought. Heaven, Earth, and the spirits and gods mostly test a person's good and evil at this very point. If a person can be without shame here in his bending and lifting, without self-reproach in his bed and in his shadow, then how can the dark room be deceived?

Wang Meixi's poem on not deceiving says: In bright room or in dark room, what doubt can there be? The heart must always hold what cannot be deceived. Ask not whether Heaven is high or the spirits hate; first of all you must fear your own knowing. Old Man Zhugen's Discourse on Fear says: In general, the human mind cannot be without something it fears. The presence or absence of a fearing heart is what distinguishes good from evil. Hence the noble person within fears his father and mother, without fears his teachers and friends; above he fears Heaven, below he fears other people. Only because his mind has something it fears does he dare not do what is contrary to propriety, and dare not stir what is contrary to right. If a single thought is shameful, his heart trembles with sorrow; if a single matter goes wrong, his face burns with embarrassment. Holding himself in caution and fear, he daily reduces his faults without even knowing it, and so he enters the realm of the noble person.

In the Song dynasty Liu Anshi, when he was already old, grew ever more renowned. At the time Liang Shicheng held power and could give life or death to men. He admired Anshi's worth, sent men to tempt him with high office, and urged him to make plans for his sons and grandsons. Anshi laughed and said, “I have provided for my sons and grandsons, and it does not come to that. In thirty years of dismissal and banishment I have never written a single stroke of ink to a powerful or noble man of the court. I wish to be a complete man of the Yuanyou era and to meet Sima Guang beneath the earth; I cannot break my rule.” He returned the letter and gave no reply.

In the Ming dynasty, Lord Dong Pu was living at home when a messenger arrived from Chu. The messenger was his own student. Earlier, Dong Pu had sealed up and sent him the examination questions he had drafted, and Dong Pu burned them, not showing them even to his son. His son later passed the examination.

In the Ming dynasty, the Minister of State Yang Zhu, a man of Wuxian, dreamed that he was wandering in a garden and ate two of its plums. When he woke he reproached himself, saying, “This is because I have ordinarily been unclear about the boundary between right and profit, and so it has come to this.” For several days he did not eat.

Long ago there was a novice monk of eight years, Miaoyan, who had already attained the spiritual powers of an arhat. He flew into the king's palace, and the queen wished to embrace him. Miaoyan said to her: “Stop, stand back. It is not fitting that your body come near a monk.” The queen replied: “You are a child, like my own son. Though I embrace you, what harm is there?” Miaoyan answered: “Judged by ordinary feeling, it is as Your Highness says. But feeling arises from the smallest beginning: it is like a single spark of fire that can burn a wilderness ten thousand li wide; it is like a trickling drop of water that can wear through the stone of Mount Tai. All things come about by gradual degrees, the few producing the many, the small growing into the great. Therefore the wise keep far from grounds of suspicion and ward off doubt, quenching the sprout and stopping the drift at its first moment.”

Yang Zhen of the Han dynasty was governor of Donglai. Passing through Changyi on the road, he was visited at night by Wang Mi, the magistrate of that county, who had once been recommended by him as a flourishing talent, and who came bearing gold as a gift. Zhen refused it. Mi said: “No one knows in the darkness of night.” Zhen said: “Heaven knows, earth knows, you know, and I know. How can you say no one knows?” Mi withdrew in shame. Yang Zhen rose to the rank of one of the Three Excellencies.

He Cheng was a skilled physician. A certain Mr. Sun had long suffered from an illness that would not heal, and summoned Cheng several times. His wife drew Cheng aside and spoke to him in secret: her husband had been ill so long that their property was all but sold up, and she was willing to give her own body in payment for the medicine. Cheng said sternly: “Lady, why speak such words? Only set your heart at ease and do not worry; I will heal him. Were I to defile myself with you, it would not only make me a petty man forever, but would cost you your great chastity as well. Even if we escaped the censure of others, the punishment of Heaven could not be evaded.” Later Cheng dreamed that he came to an official hall, where a spirit said to him: “You have done good service in the practice of medicine, and you did not take advantage of a woman in her distress. The High God grants you an office and fifty thousand strings of cash.” Before long the crown prince fell ill, and when a physician was sought, Cheng was found; one dose of medicine cured him. Office and money were bestowed on him exactly in the number promised.

Stored in the mind, it is virtue; manifested in action, it is merit; increased from few to many, it is accumulation; raised from low to high, it is piling up. Virtue that is not accumulated does not become lofty; merit that is not piled up does not become great. If only one can be earnest and diligent, like a farmer longing for the harvest, and urgent and eager, like a merchant pursuing profit — today accumulating one virtue, tomorrow accumulating another; today piling up one merit, tomorrow piling up another — then the thousand three hundred good deeds required of a celestial immortal need only four years of practice, and the three hundred good deeds required of an earthly immortal need only one year. The trouble is simply that people cannot keep at it, and fear they will give up midway. Their delusion is deep-set and their habitual defilements hard to remove; principle is no match for desire, and the good conscience flashes out only to die again, so that in the end they never find the occasion for doing good. I only hope that all in the world who arouse the vow to do good will possess a single true and trusting heart, a courageous heart, a heart of diligent progress, and a heart firm and enduring. Do not stint your wealth and stop halfway; do not fear ridicule and doubt yourself; do not cling to comfort and ease and so fail to rouse yourself; do not be dragged about by selfish desire and so lack firm resolve; do not merely make a show of discharging your duty and then abandon it halfway; do not rest content in small achievements and feel fully satisfied; do not vainly aim at what is high and remote while neglecting real practice; do not shrink from a task because it is great; do not slight a good because it is small; do not push a duty onto others because you are busy; do not hoard your reputation and standing and so fail to rescue those in trouble; do not strive only where you are seen and slacken where you are unseen; do not strive in your outward actions and neglect your speech; do not offer fine words while your practice does not match them; do not hold fast in ordinary times and neglect the moment of trial; do not be diligent at the beginning and idle at the end. Do not avoid suspicion; do not avoid resentment; do not drift along; do not break off; do not be reckless; do not seek reward; do not strive for fame. Whenever you meet with any good deed at all, take it up with joy, and see it through every turn and difficulty until it is accomplished — only then are you one who truly holds and practices the seed.

The Perfected Lady Zixu said: Long ago there was Mr. Fu, who loved the Way from childhood. He entered a stone chamber on Mount Jiao and dwelt there for three years, when he suddenly met the Great Ultimate Perfected One, who gave him a wooden drill and set him to bore through a great flat rock. The Perfected One warned him: “When the stone is pierced, I will ferry you across.” The stone was more than five feet thick, and Fu drilled without cease. When forty-seven years had passed, the stone was suddenly pierced through, and the Great Ultimate Perfected One indeed came to ferry him across. Now the piling up of virtue and the accumulation of merit does not really consist in drilling stone, yet by this we may reason: the trouble with people is that they will not do the work, or that they draw the line and give up halfway. Where there is a will, the work is in the end accomplished. Is this not clear proof?

Ge Fan, prefect of Zhenjiang in the Song dynasty, performed several good deeds every day without fail for forty years. When someone asked him about it, Fan said: “I do nothing special; I simply do one or two things each day that benefit others.” Pointing to the footrest beside his seat, he said: “When an object like this is set crooked, it bruises people's feet, so I straighten it for them; when a person is thirsty, I give him a cup of water. All these are beneficial acts. From ministers and chancellors down to beggars, everyone can do them. Only one must keep at it long, and then there is benefit in it.”

Yang Xun served as judicial officer of Kuizhou and accumulated merit and virtue, emulating Zhou Chi in practicing the ten kinds of benefit set forth in the Taishang Ganying Pian. First, he gathered up infants abandoned in the streets and markets, hired people to care for them, and when they reached the age of fifteen, if anyone wished to acknowledge them, returned them to their parents for a happy reunion. Second, each year beginning on the third day of the eleventh month, he took in beggars and the poor, those over sixty and those under fifteen, into a relief hall of his own household, giving each daily a pint of rice and fifteen coppers; after three full months he let them go their own way to seek a living. Third, he freely distributed proved and effective medicines to save people from the suffering of illness. Fourth, he gave coffins to families with no means to bury their dead. Fifth, when maidservants grew up, he did not count the cost of their purchase but gave them a measure of clothing and money and let them marry as they wished. Sixth, he was single-minded in abstaining from killing and in protecting and saving living beings: whenever he met with creatures that fly or walk, great or small, he bought them back and set them free. Seventh, whenever a year of famine came, he bought grain dear and sold it cheap to relieve the poor. Eighth, when the sacred images in temples and monasteries were damaged or peeling, he repaired and restored them; where bridges and roads were broken, or ditches and channels blocked, he had them all put in order. Ninth, when scholars and officials from distant regions were stranded, he helped them with funds to return home. Tenth, as an official he redressed wrongs and righted injustices, extending his own feelings to others, relieving the distressed and supporting the endangered, cutting down the strong and bringing peace to the weak. Afterwards his son Yang Chun came first in the whole empire in the examinations. Those who do not understand the profit of the autumn harvest, seeing another sow seed, wonder: “Why throw away what could be eaten into the mud?” Those who do not understand the field of blessing are just the same. There is a proverb: Plant bamboo and you get shoots; plant lotus and you get roots. All of us who share this work already know it. Take care not to grudge the seed.

Dou Yujun of Yanshan in the Later Zhou was a remonstrance official in the time of the Five Dynasties. At thirty he had no son, and he dreamed that his grandfather said to him: “You have no son and your years are not long. You must quickly do good.” Yujun assented. He was by nature a man of generous heart. Earlier a household servant had stolen two hundred strings of cash and, fearing discovery, since he had a daughter still young, wrote out a deed in his own hand and tied it to the girl's arm, saying that she was sold forever to this house in repayment of the money owed, and then fled far away. Yujun pitied her, burned the deed, and charged his wife to raise her well. When she reached the age of binding her hair, he gave two hundred strings of cash and chose a good match to marry her to. The servant heard of it and wept with gratitude; he came back and waited for his punishment, but Yujun set the matter aside and asked nothing about it. Again, on New Year's Day at the Yanqing Monastery he picked up two ingots of gold and ten ounces of silver, carried them home, and returning to the monastery the next day waited for the owner to come back and restored them to him, and the man was able to redeem his father from punishment. Again, when kinsmen of his own clan or relatives by marriage had deaths they could not afford to bury, he gave money to bury them, twenty-seven in all; when daughters could not be married, he gave money to marry them, twenty-eight in all. Old friends in poverty he lent money to, great or small according to the case, so that they could trade, and more than a few dozen families lived through his kindness. Worthy scholars from every quarter who relied on his recommendation cannot be counted. He also built forty rooms of an academy south of his house, gathered a thousand scrolls of books, and respectfully engaged scholars of literary culture and practice as teachers, so that the orphaned and poor of every region who had the will to learn might come of their own accord, and he provided them generously with grain. Thus his sons daily widened their knowledge and understanding. Each year the duke measured his income, and after setting aside what was needed for sacrifices and daily use, he gave it all away to relieve others. His household was of the utmost frugality and simplicity: no ornaments of gold or jade, no concubine clothed in silk. Later he again dreamed that his grandfather said to him: “You had no son and your span was short, but in these several years you have accumulated hidden virtue, and your name is already entered in the heavenly records. The High God has specially extended your life by three twelve-year cycles, and your five sons shall be honored and prosperous, with blessing and long life. After your end you shall serve as a Perfected One of the Cavern Heavens.” His grandfather also said: “The principle of yin and yang is on the whole not different. The retribution of good and evil is sometimes issued in this present life and sometimes repaid in a life to come. The net of Heaven is vast, and though its mesh is wide, nothing slips through. Of this there can be no doubt.” The duke accumulated hidden merit all the more, and his five sons and eight grandsons all became honored. He lived to the age of eighty-two, and one evening, chatting and laughing with relatives and friends, he passed away.

Han Qi, Duke of Wei in the Song dynasty, rose to high office while still young. Above all he was able to show filial reverence to his forebears, and he raised and cared for his nephews as though they were his own sons; he clothed and fed a hundred mouths of his clan. Whatever favor or gift he received he first gave to his kin. He served as chancellor through three reigns, and whatever was of benefit to the state and the altars of soil and grain, he knew nothing he would not do. He roused his loyalty and courage and set the world at peace. He taught his sons by the right method, with a strictness that could not be transgressed, and his words and actions all issued from perfect sincerity. He relieved the urgent needs of others, and when his strength fell short he gave up his own clothing, food, and treasured playthings, even unclasping his wife's hairpins and earrings to give away. The descendants of old friends in cold and poverty depended on him for their living, often several dozen households. When he was military commissioner of Yizhou, a great famine came, and he reduced and remitted the tax grain, called on people to contribute grain, and also recruited strong men as soldiers, so that when one man took up service several mouths could live. In the Mingdao era, on account of the damage of the disaster, he urged and induced people to deliver grain, which was returned to the ever-normal granaries, and issued porridge to the lower households, saving more than one million nine hundred thousand famine victims. When he governed Bingzhou, the custom of Hedong was to use cremation; the duke bought open ground so that people could be buried there. In the days when he governed Daming, he looked into every matter himself, great or small, and even when ill he had cases decided at his bedside. Someone urged him to delegate the government to subordinate officials. The duke said: “Lawsuits are the great affair of a person's life: life and death, gain and loss, are decided by a single word. How can one be other than careful? I am ever afraid of not doing all I can, and would I dare entrust it to another?” Someone presented him with two jade cups, and the duke took them for a hundred pieces of gold. Whenever he entertained guests he set out a special table and placed the cups there, resting on brocade. One day when he feasted the grain commissioner, a petty clerk knocked the table over by mistake and the cups were broken. Everyone was astonished, but the duke's expression did not change. He said to his guests with a smile: “Everything has its fixed number, whether it is made or destroyed.” Then he turned to the clerk and said: “You did it by mistake, not on purpose. Do not be alarmed.” The guests all sighed in admiration. When the duke was in command at Wuding, he was writing at night and a soldier attended him with a candle. The soldier happened to look away, and the flame burned the duke's beard. The duke only brushed his beard with his sleeve and went on writing as before. After a little while he looked around and saw that the man had already been replaced by another soldier. Fearing that the officer in charge would flog him, the duke quickly called him back, saying: “Do not change him. He can hold the candle well enough now.” When people heard of it, there was no one who was not moved and filled with admiration. The duke died full of years. At his death a great star fell with a sound like thunder, and he was given the posthumous title Zhongxian. His five sons were honored and prominent, and his descendants flourished beyond compare.

Thirty li north of the city of Shaoxing in the Ming dynasty lies the open sea. With every tide the waters poured in and drowned the fields and crops. In the Jiajing era, Duke Tang Duzhai of Mianzhu in Shu was prefect of the prefecture, and he exhausted his mind and strength to build more than a hundred li of sea embankment and to make twenty-eight sluice gates, so that the waters might be opened and closed according to the season; from that time on there was a rich harvest every year, and the people relied on it forever. When he was later transferred to another post, the scholars and common people wept and wailed until the sound shook the heavens, and they set up a shrine for him at Sanjiang, where sacrifices have continued without interruption to this day.

Mr. Jiao of the Eastern Capital had gone three generations without a legitimate heir, and so he became a traveling merchant, seeking out perfected men everywhere to ask the cause. He met an old monk, who said: “There are three reasons for having no son. First, the ancestors had no virtue and the man himself has no good conduct. Second, the years and fates of husband and wife may offend against prohibitions. Third, the spirit is not guarded and the blood of the wife and concubines is cold.” Jiao said: “Virtue, conduct, years and fate can all be received and upheld. But what method can cure cold blood?” The monk said: “It is not hard. First pile up virtue and accumulate merit, then nourish your body, and after three years come to Mount Wutai, where you shall be given a rare prescription.” From that time on Jiao constantly did what was convenient for others, accumulating hidden merit in every way, bestowing kindness and spreading virtue for three years, and then he went to Wutai. He did not meet the old monk, but suddenly saw a novice holding a scroll in his hand, who said: “My teacher sends word to you, sir. Your merit is accomplished and your practice complete. Go home and compound the medicine; take it with a sincere heart, and you shall surely have sons and grandsons of wealth and honor, born according to your wish.” Afterwards a son was born, the young Mr. Jiao, but the son he bore was again unworthy. Bitterly regretting how he could have thus damaged his virtue, the young Mr. Jiao also went to Wutai, where he saw the novice, who said: “My teacher sends word: why come to ask? Only do as your father did, and the foolish shall of themselves become worthy and the poor of themselves become rich.” The young Mr. Jiao said: “That the poor should become rich is a matter of fate. But folly is the original nature of a person; how can it be turned to worth?” The novice said: “In former times the five sons of the Dou family were all born with incomplete bodies. Afterwards he spread kindness and virtue all the more, and they all became whole and well, and all passed the examinations. This is manifest and without error.” The young Mr. Jiao thanked him and went home, and believing and practicing his words, after twenty years he had many heirs, and they were honored. People today all know that the five sons of the Dou family rose in succession to honor and glory, but how do they know that at birth they were all diseased and crippled, that they were first made safe by accumulation and afterwards met with their fortune through merit and virtue? So easy is the sympathetic communion between Heaven and man. Therefore I have recorded this at length here as surety for piling up virtue and accumulating merit. May those who have the will keep their hearts firm and never slacken.

In the Ming dynasty Yuan Liaofan's chapter on accumulating good says: The Book of Changes states that the family that piles up good deeds will surely have abundant blessings. Long ago, when the Yan family was about to give a daughter in marriage to Shulianghe, they recounted at length how his ancestors had accumulated virtue, and foreknew that among his descendants there must be one who would rise. Confucius praised the great filial piety of Shun, saying that the ancestral temple would offer him sacrifice and his descendants would preserve his line. Both are perfect teachings. Let us test them by past events. Yang Rong, Junior Preceptor of the Heir Apparent, was a man of Jianning. His family had for generations made its living by ferrying people across. Once rain fell long and the stream rose, and the rushing flood destroyed the people's houses; those who drowned floated downstream, while the other boats all scooped up goods. Only the Junior Preceptor's great-grandfather and grandfather saved people and took nothing of the goods at all. The country people mocked them for fools. By the time the Junior Preceptor's father was born, the household was gradually well-off, and a spirit in the form of a Daoist said to him: “Your father and grandfather have hidden merit, and their descendants shall be honored and prominent. You should bury your dead in such-and-such a place.” So he buried them as directed, and that is what is now called the White Rabbit Grave. Afterwards the Junior Preceptor was born; at twenty he passed the examinations and rose to the rank of one of the Three Excellencies, and the same offices were conferred on his great-grandfather and grandfather. His sons and grandsons were honored and flourishing, and to this day many of them are worthy men. Yang Zicheng of Yin was at first a county clerk, kindly of heart, who kept the law fairly. At that time the county magistrate was stern, and having flogged a prisoner until the blood ran before him, his anger was still unspent. Yang knelt and pleaded to soften him. The magistrate said: “What can I do about this man? He transgresses the law and violates principle; one cannot help being angry.” Zicheng bowed his head to the ground and said: “When those above lose the Way, the people have long been scattered. If one finds out the true circumstances, one should pity and not rejoice. Rejoicing is not even permissible — how much less anger?” The magistrate's face cleared. His family was very poor, and he took nothing of any gifts or offerings. When prisoners lacked food, he would often find some way to relieve them. One day several new prisoners were waiting to be fed, and his own household was short of rice. If he gave to the prisoners his family would have nothing to eat; if he looked to his own, the prisoners were pitiable. He consulted his wife. His wife said: “Where do the prisoners come from?” He said: “They come from Hangzhou, enduring hunger all along the road, their faces the color of vegetables.” So they took away their own rice and cooked porridge to feed the prisoners. Afterwards two sons were born, the elder named Shouchen and the younger Shouzhi; they became junior and senior vice ministers of the Ministry of Personnel. The eldest grandson became vice minister of the Ministry of Justice, and the second grandson became a surveillance commissioner of Sichuan; both were famous ministers. Chu Ting and Dezheng of today are also of his line. In former times, during the Zhengtong era, Deng Maoqi raised rebellion in Fujian, and a great many scholars and common people followed the rebels. The court sent Zhang Kai, the grand censor of Yin county, on a southern campaign, and he took the rebels by stratagem. Afterwards it appointed Xie, a secretary of the provincial administration commission, to search out and kill the rebel party on the eastern road. Xie asked for the register of those who had joined the rebels, and secretly searched out all who had not joined them, giving them small white cloth flags and agreeing that on the day the troops arrived they should plant the flags at their doorways; he warned the soldiers not to kill recklessly, and a whole ten thousand lives were saved. Afterwards Xie's son Xie Qian came first in the palace examination and became a chief councillor, and his grandson Xie Pi came third in the palace examination. In the Lin family of Putian, an old mother of an earlier generation loved to do good and constantly made rice cakes to give to people; whoever asked she gave to them, without ever showing weariness. A spirit in the form of a Daoist asked for six or seven cakes every morning, and the mother gave them day after day, for three whole years as though it were a single day, so that he knew her sincerity. He then said to her: “I have eaten your rice cakes for three years. How shall I repay you? Behind the prefectural office there is a plot of ground; bury your dead there, and your sons and grandsons shall rise in office to the number of a pint of hemp seeds.” Her son buried her as he directed. In the very first generation nine of the family passed the examinations, and for successive generations their caps and tassels were exceedingly numerous. In Fujian there is a saying that where there is no Lin family, no examination list is posted.

The father of the Hanlin scholar Feng Zhuoan was a student of the county school. Rising early on a bitter winter day to go to his studies, he met a man lying in the snow, and when he touched him he was half frozen. So he took off his own padded fur robe and clothed him in it, then lifted him up and carried him home and revived him. He dreamed that a spirit told him: “You have saved a human life, out of the utmost sincerity of heart. I shall send Han Qi to be your son.” When Zhuoan was born, he was therefore named Qi. Ying, a minister of the Ministry of Personnel from Taizhou, pursued his studies in the mountains in his prime. At night the ghosts gathered with their howling and often frightened people, but the duke was not afraid. One evening he heard a ghost say: “A certain woman, because her husband has long been away and has not returned, is being pressed by her parents-in-law to marry another man. Tomorrow night she will hang herself here, and I shall get my substitute.” The duke secretly sold land and got four ounces of silver, then forged a letter from her husband and sent the silver home. When her parents saw the letter they doubted it because the handwriting was not like his; then they said: “The letter may be false, but the silver cannot be false. We may suppose our son is safe and well.” So the woman did not marry. Her husband afterwards returned, and husband and wife preserved each other as at the first. The duke again heard a ghost say: “I was to get my substitute, but this scholar has ruined my affair.” Another ghost beside him said: “Why do you not bring calamity on him?” He said: “The High God, because this man's heart is good, has appointed him to be a minister of hidden virtue. How could I bring calamity on him?” Lord Ying strove all the harder, daily cultivating good and daily thickening his virtue. When a year of famine came he would donate grain to relieve the people; when kinsmen were in urgent need he would find some way to sustain them; when he met with perverse and violent treatment he would turn back on himself and reproach himself, and calmly and gladly accept it. His sons and grandsons who passed the examinations are many indeed today. Xu Fengzhu, whose name was Shi, of Changshu, had a father who was always wealthy. When a year of famine happened to come, he was first to remit the rents, as a leader for the whole county, and he also distributed grain to relieve the poor and lacking. At night he heard a ghost singing at his gate: “A thousand times no lie, ten thousand times no lie: the scholar of the Xu family has become a provincial graduate.” The cry went on and on, night after night without ceasing. That year Fengzhu indeed passed the provincial examination. His father accordingly accumulated virtue all the more, diligent and unwearied: he built bridges, repaired roads, fed monks, and received the multitude, and whatever was of benefit he did with all his heart. Afterwards the ghost was again heard singing at the gate: “A thousand times no lie, ten thousand times no lie: the provincial graduate of the Xu family will rise all the way to the censorate.” Fengzhu ended his career as governor of the two Zhe. Duke Tu Kangxi of Jiaxing was at first a secretary of the Ministry of Justice. He lodged in the prison and questioned the prisoners in detail about their circumstances, finding a number of innocent men. He did not take the credit as his own, but secretly set out the matter in a memorial and reported it to the chief minister. Afterwards, at the autumn assizes, the chief minister drew out his words to interrogate the prisoners, and none failed to submit. More than ten who had been wronged were released, and for a time everyone in the capital praised the minister's wisdom. The duke further reported: “Under the very walls of the capital there are still many wronged people; in the breadth of the four seas and among the multitude of the people, how can there be none who are wronged? It would be well to send a remission officer every five years to verify the facts and redress them.” The minister memorialized the throne, and his proposal was approved. At that time the duke too was in the ranks of the remission officers. He dreamed that a spirit told him: “Your fate holds no son. But this proposal to reduce punishments accords deeply with the heart of Heaven. The High God grants you three sons, all to wear purple and gird gold.” That night his wife conceived. Afterwards were born Yingxun, Yingkun, and Yingjun, all prominent officials.

Bao Ping of Jiaxing, whose courtesy name was Xinzhi, had a father who was prefect of Chiyang. He had seven sons, and Ping was the youngest; he married into the Yuan family of Pinghu as a resident son-in-law, and was on most intimate terms with my own father. He was widely learned and of high talent, but repeatedly failed the examinations. He set his mind on the teachings of the two schools. One day, traveling east on Lake Mao, he happened by chance on a village temple and saw an image of Guanyin standing drenched and exposed. He at once opened his bag and took out ten pieces of gold, giving them to the presiding monk to have the hall repaired. The monk told him that the work was great and the silver little, and could not be finished. So he took four bolts of pine cloth and seven garments from his chest and gave them to him, among them a new padded garment of ramie. His servant begged him to keep it back. Ping said: “As long as the sacred image comes to no harm, what does it matter if I go bare?” The monk, with tears falling, said: “To give silver and clothing and cloth is not so hard; but this single thought of yours, how is it to be had?” When the work was done, he brought his aged father to visit and they lodged in the temple. The duke dreamed that the temple guardian spirit came to thank him, saying: “Your son shall enjoy the emoluments of the world.” Afterwards his son Bian and his grandson Chengfang both passed the examinations and became prominent officials. The father of Zhi Li of Jiashan was a clerk of the judicial section. A prisoner had been wrongfully condemned to a heavy punishment, and he pitied him at heart and wished to save his life. The prisoner said to his wife: “Commissioner Zhi is so kind. I am ashamed that I have nothing to repay him with. Tomorrow invite him out to the countryside, and give your body to serve him. He may then be willing to use his influence, and I may live.” His wife wept and obeyed. When he came, the wife came out herself to urge wine on him and told him her husband's meaning. Zhi would not listen, but in the end did all he could to clear the man and reverse the verdict. When the prisoner left the prison, husband and wife came to his gate and bowed in thanks, saying: “Such profound virtue as yours, sir, is rare in these late times. You have no son; I have a young daughter, and I send her to you as a humble wife. This is what propriety allows.” Zhi prepared the proper betrothal gifts and took her. A son was born, Li, who at twenty took first place in the provincial examination and rose to be a Hanlin archivist. Li begot Gao, and Gao begot Lu, both of whom were presented as tribute students and became instructors. Lu begot Dalun, who passed the examinations. Now these ten examples differ in what was done, but they come home to the good alone. If we speak of them more finely still, then good has true and false, straightforward and devious, hidden and open, right and wrong, partial and correct, half and full, great and small, difficult and easy, and all of these must be discerned deeply. To do good without fathoming principle is to think one is practicing while in fact one is creating karma, wasting bitter effort and gaining nothing. What is true and what is false? Long ago several scholars of the Confucian school came to visit the monk Zhongfeng and asked: “The Buddhists teach that good and evil bring their retribution as a shadow follows a shape. But now a certain man is good, and his sons and grandsons do not rise; a certain man is evil, and his house flourishes. The Buddha's words are groundless.” Zhongfeng said: “While worldly feeling is not yet washed away and the true eye is not yet opened, it happens again and again that one takes good for evil and points to evil as good. Do you not regret that your own right and wrong are turned upside down, but instead resent that Heaven's retribution is uneven?” The company said: “How can good and evil be so reversed?” Zhongfeng asked them to try to describe the cases. One said that to revile and beat others is evil and to respect and be courteous to others is good. Zhongfeng said: “That is not necessarily so.” One said that to covet wealth and take it wrongly is evil, and to be honest and upright is good. Zhongfeng said: “That is not necessarily so.” The company described case after case, and Zhongfeng said to all of them that it was not so. Then they asked him for instruction. Zhongfeng told them: “Good is what benefits others; evil is what benefits oneself. If it benefits others, then even reviling and beating are good. If it benefits oneself, then even respecting and being courteous to others is evil. Therefore when a person does good, to benefit others is public, and what is public is true; to benefit oneself is private, and what is private is false. Again, what is rooted in the heart is true, and what imitates outward traces is false. Again, what is done without contrivance is true, and what is done with contrivance is false. All of these one must examine for oneself.”

What is straightforward and what is devious? People today, seeing a cautious and agreeable gentleman, all call him good and accept him, while the sages would rather take the ardent and the scrupulous. As for the cautious and agreeable gentleman, though the whole village may like him, he must be considered a thief of virtue. Thus the world's good and evil are plainly the reverse of the sages'. Extending this one point, every kind of acceptance and rejection is sure to be mistaken. The way Heaven, Earth, ghosts, and spirits bless the good and bring calamity on the licentious agrees with the sages' right and wrong, and does not agree with the world's acceptance and rejection. Therefore anyone who wishes to accumulate good must never follow his eyes and ears, but only from the hidden and subtle place of the mind's source silently wash himself clean. If it is purely a heart of saving the world, that is straightforward; if there is the least trace of a heart courting the world, that is devious. If it is purely a heart of loving others, that is straightforward; if there is the least trace of a heart resenting the world, that is devious. If it is purely a heart of respecting others, that is straightforward; if there is the least trace of a heart trifling with the world, that is devious. All of these must be discerned minutely. What is right and what is wrong? The law of the state of Lu provided that if a man of Lu ransomed a fellow countryman held as a slave among the feudal lords, he should receive gold from the treasury. Zigong ransomed men and did not accept the gold. Confucius heard of it and was displeased, saying: “Si has erred. When a sage undertakes a matter, it may change the customs and transform the manners, and his teaching may be applied among the common people; it is not merely a matter of suiting himself. Now in Lu the rich are few and the poor are many. To accept the gold is to be thought dishonest; how then shall anyone ransom men? From this day on, no one will ransom men from the feudal lords again.” Zilu saved a man from drowning, and the man thanked him with an ox, and Zilu accepted it. Confucius said with joy: “From this day on, many in Lu will save men from drowning.” Seen with worldly eyes, Zigong's refusal of the gold was the finer and Zilu's acceptance of the ox the poorer; but Confucius approved You and dismissed Si. Hence we know that when a person does good, the question is not the act as it now appears but the harm it may flow into, not the moment but the long run, not the one man but the whole world. Though the present act be good, if its flow is enough to harm others, then it seems good and is in truth not good. Though the present act be not good, if its flow is enough to save others, then it is not good and is in truth good. Yet this speaks only of one kind of case. Others, such as rightness that is not right, propriety that is not proper, faithfulness that is not faithful, and kindness that is not kind, must all be judged. What is partial and what is correct? Long ago Duke Lu Wenyi, having just resigned the chancellorship and returned to his home village, was looked up to throughout the land as Mount Tai and the North Star. A certain villager, drunk, reviled him. The duke did not stir, and said to his servant: “He is drunk; do not quarrel with him.” He shut his gate and declined to see him. A year later the man committed a capital crime and entered prison. The duke then regretted it, saying: “Had I then made some small matter of it and sent him to the authorities for reproof and punishment, he might have been checked by a small penalty and avoided a great one. At the time I only wished to keep a generous heart, and did not expect to foster his evil to such a pass.” This is a case of doing an evil deed out of a good heart. There is also the doing of a good deed out of an evil heart. For example, a certain family was very rich, and when a year of famine came the poor snatched grain in the marketplace in broad daylight. They reported it to the county, and the county took no notice; the poor grew more reckless. So the family privately seized them and subjected them to hardship and humiliation, and the crowd was at last quieted; otherwise there would almost have been a riot. Thus good is what is correct and evil is what is partial, and everyone knows this. But to do an evil deed out of a good heart is the partial within the correct, and to do a good deed out of an evil heart is the correct within the partial. This one must not fail to know.

What is half and what is full? The Book of Changes says: If good is not accumulated, it is not enough to make a name; if evil is not accumulated, it is not enough to destroy the self. The Book of Documents says that the crimes of Shang were full to overflowing. It is like storing things in a vessel: gather diligently and it is filled; be slack and do not gather and it is not filled. That is one account. Long ago, a certain man's daughter went into a temple wishing to give, but she had no wealth, only two coins, which she donated. The abbot himself performed the repentance for her. Later she entered the palace and became rich and honored, and brought several thousand pieces of gold into the temple to give. The presiding monk only told his disciple to dedicate the merit. She therefore asked: “Before, I gave two coins and you yourself performed the repentance; now I give several thousand pieces of gold and you do not dedicate the merit. Why?” He said: “Before, the gift was thin but the heart of giving was utterly true; unless the old monk himself performed the repentance, it was not enough to repay the virtue. Now the gift is thick but the heart of giving is not as keen as before; it is enough for another to perform the repentance in my place.” Thus the thousand pieces of gold were half, and the two coins were full. Zhongli taught the patriarch Lü the elixir that turns iron into gold, which could relieve the world. Lü asked: “Will it ever change back?” He said: “After five hundred years it will return to its original substance.” Lü said: “Then it will harm the people of five hundred years from now. I do not wish to do it.” He said: “To cultivate immortality one must accumulate three thousand deeds. With this one word of yours, the three thousand deeds are already complete.” That is another account. For example, when one relieves others with wealth, if inwardly one does not see oneself, outwardly one does not see the recipient, and in between one does not see the thing given, this is called the three wheels being empty in essence, and is called the mind being pure. Then a single pint of grain can plant boundless blessing, and a single coin can dissolve the offenses of a thousand kalpas. If this mind is not forgotten, then even ten thousand yi of gold will not fill up one's blessing. That is another account. What is great and what is small? Long ago Wei Zhongda held a post in the academy. He was seized and taken to the underworld, where the presiding judge ordered a clerk to present the two records of good and evil. When they came, the record of his evil filled the courtyard, while the record of his good was a slip no bigger than a chopstick. A scale was called for and they were weighed, and the record that filled the courtyard was the lighter, while the slip was the heavier. Zhongda said: “I am not yet forty; how could I have so many faults?” He was told: “A single thought that is not right counts as one. It does not wait for the deed.” He then asked what was written on the scroll. He was told: “Once the court undertook a great work, the building of the stone bridge of the Three Mountains. You submitted a memorial dissuading it. This is the draft of that memorial.” Zhongda said: “Though I spoke of it, the court did not follow; what good did it do in the matter? How could it have such power?” He was told: “Though the court did not follow it, that single thought of yours already rested on the ten thousand people. Had it been followed, the power of the good would have been greater still.” Therefore when the will rests on the whole world and the state, then though the good be small it is great; if it rests on one's own person, then though it be much it is small.

What is difficult and what is easy? The earlier Confucians said that to overcome the self one must overcome it at the very place that is hardest to overcome. When the Master discussed practicing benevolence, he too said to begin with what is difficult. It must be like old Mr. Shu of Jiangxi, who gave up the stipend he had saved over two years to pay off another man's official debt and so preserved a husband and wife whole; and like old Mr. Zhang of Handan, who gave up the money he had painfully saved over ten years to redeem another's ransom and so kept a man's wife and children alive. Both are cases of being able to give where giving is hard. And like old Mr. Jin of Zhenjiang, who, though old and without a son, could not bear to take a young girl as his concubine and returned her to her neighbor: this is being able to endure where enduring is hard. Therefore Heaven's blessing came down on them with special richness. In general, those who have wealth and power find it easy to establish virtue; to find it easy and yet not do it is called casting oneself away. For the poor and lowly it is hard to create blessing; to do it where it is hard is what makes it precious. To relieve the multitude according to circumstance has very many kinds; to speak of them in outline, there are about ten. First, to be a helper of others in doing good. Second, to keep a heart of love and respect. Third, to complete the beauties of others. Fourth, to urge others to do good. Fifth, to rescue others in crisis and danger. Sixth, to undertake great works of benefit. Seventh, to give away wealth and create blessing. Eighth, to protect and uphold the true Dharma. Ninth, to revere and honor elders and superiors. Tenth, to cherish the lives of living things. What is being a helper of others in doing good? Long ago Shun was by the river and saw the fishermen all contending for the deep pools and rich waters, while the old and weak fished in the rushing currents and shallow shoals. He pitied them with a grieving heart and went to fish there himself. When he saw those who contended, he concealed their faults and did not speak of them; when he saw one who yielded, he praised and spread his example and took it as a model. Within a year all were yielding to one another the deep pools and rich waters. With Shun's wisdom and discernment, could he not have spoken a single word to teach the crowd? Yet he did not teach by words but turned them by his own person. This is the painstaking care of a master workman. When we live in this latter age, we must not use our own strengths to cover others, nor use our own goodness to make others look small, nor use our own many abilities to trap others. Draw in your talents and wisdom, as though you had none and were empty. When you see the faults of others, bear with them and cover them over, so that on the one hand they may be able to mend, and on the other they may have some scruple and not dare to indulge themselves. When you see in others some small excellence worth taking or some small good worth recording, turn about and set yourself aside to follow it, and sing its praises and spread them widely. In all the affairs of daily life, whenever you speak a word or do a deed, let no thought whatever arise for your own sake; let it all be to set a standard for others. This is the magnanimity of the great man who regards the whole world as public. What is keeping a heart of love and respect? Looking at the outward traces, the gentleman and the petty man are often easily confused. Only at the single point of what is kept in the heart are good and evil poles apart, as plainly opposed as black and white. Therefore it is said that the reason the gentleman differs from others is what he keeps in his heart. What the gentleman keeps in his heart is only a heart of love and respect for others. For people differ as kin and stranger, noble and base, wise and foolish, worthy and unworthy; the ten thousand kinds are uneven, yet all are my brothers and sisters, all are one body with me. Who among them is not to be respected and loved? To love and respect the multitude is to love and respect the sages and worthies. To be able to penetrate the minds of the multitude is to be able to penetrate the minds of the sages and worthies. Why? The mind of the sages and worthies desired from the first that this world and its people should each find their proper place. If I join love to love and respect to respect and so bring peace to the people of a whole age, then I am bringing them peace on behalf of the sages and worthies.

What is completing the beauties of others? Jade in the rough stone, if it is thrown and cast about, is rubble; if it is carved and polished, it is a tablet of honor. Therefore whenever one sees another do a good deed, or sees that a person's aspiration is worth taking and his capacity can be advanced, one must lead him on and support him and bring him to completion. Either give him encouragement, or sustain him, or clear him of false accusations and share the burden of slander against him; see to it that he is established before you stop.
