In general people hate those who are not of their own kind. In any village the good are few and the not good are many. A good person amid the common run finds it hard to stand on his own; moreover, the spirited and outstanding often do not much cultivate appearances and are easily picked at. Hence good works are often easily ruined and good people often slandered. Only the benevolent and the mature correct them and support them on both sides, and their merit and virtue are the greatest. What is urging others to do good? Being born a human, who has no good conscience? But the roads of the world are a drudgery, and one most easily drowns in them. Whenever you deal with others, you should find a skillful way to jog them awake and open their delusion, like rousing someone from a great dream in the long night, like pulling someone long sunk in affliction up into coolness and clarity. The benefit of this is the most wide-reaching of all. Han Yu said: To urge people for a time, use the mouth; to urge people for a hundred generations, use a book. Compared with being a helper of others in doing good, this works through outward traces, yet it prescribes medicine to match the illness and sometimes has marvelous effect, and so must not be discarded. Whether one has spoken amiss or missed the right person, one should turn back and examine one's own wisdom. What is rescuing others in crisis and danger? Hardship and adversity come to everyone at some time. When you happen to meet with it, you should feel it as pain and sickness in your own body and hasten to rescue and relieve. Either by a word you clear away an injustice that has bent someone down, or by many means you relieve someone in unending distress. Master Cui said: Kindness need not be great; it is enough to go to a person's urgent need. That is truly the word of a benevolent man. What is undertaking great works of benefit? Small, within a single village; great, within a whole city: whatever is of benefit is most fitting to undertake and build. Either open a channel to lead water, or raise a dike against harm, or repair bridges and roads for the convenience of travelers, or give tea and food to relieve hunger and thirst. Urge others on as occasion offers and join strength to build it. Do not avoid suspicion; do not decline toil or resentment. What is giving away wealth and creating blessing? Of the ten thousand practices of the Buddhist gate, giving is first. What is called giving is nothing but the single word to let go. For one who has penetrated, inwardly he lets go of the six senses, outwardly he lets go of the six dusts; of all that he has, there is nothing he does not let go. If one cannot yet do this, then begin by giving of wealth. The people of the world take food and clothing as their life, and so wealth is what they value most. If I let it go, inwardly I break my own stinginess and outwardly I relieve others in need. At first it is forced; in the end it is easy and calm. It is the best thing for washing away private feeling and removing grasping and miserliness. What is protecting and upholding the true Dharma? The Dharma is the eye of all living beings through ten thousand generations. Without the true Dharma, how could one assist and participate in Heaven and Earth? How could one shape and complete the ten thousand things? How could one escape the dust and leave bondage? How could one pass through the world and go beyond it? Therefore whenever you see the temples and images of the sages and worthies, or sutras and books and records, you should revere them and repair and adorn them. And as for proclaiming and raising up the true Dharma and so repaying the Buddha's kindness above, you should strive at this above all.

What is revering and honoring elders and superiors? The father and elder brothers in the home, the ruler and elders of the state, and all who are advanced in years, in virtue, in position, or in understanding, should be attended with special care. In the home, when you serve your parents, let there be deep love and a gentle countenance, a soft voice and a lowly bearing, until it becomes second nature; this is the very root of the harmonious vapor that moves Heaven. Going out to serve your ruler, in whatever matter you undertake, do not say that your ruler does not know and so give yourself free rein; in punishing any person, do not say that your ruler does not see and so put on airs of authority. To serve one's ruler as one serves Heaven: this was the settled teaching of the ancients. In these places hidden virtue is most at stake. Look at the families of the loyal and the filial: among their sons and grandsons there are none who do not continue far and flourish. Take the utmost care in this. What is cherishing the lives of living things? The only thing that makes a person a person is this heart of compassionate pity. Those who seek benevolence seek this; those who accumulate virtue accumulate this. The Rites of Zhou says that in the first month of spring the sacrificial victims should not be female. Mencius said that the gentleman keeps away from the kitchen, and this is how one preserves whole one's heart of compassionate pity. Therefore the elders had the precept of the four things not to eat: what one has heard being killed, one does not eat; what one has seen being killed, one does not eat; what one has raised oneself, one does not eat; what has been killed expressly for oneself, one does not eat. Students who cannot yet cut off meat should begin by keeping this precept, and gradually advancing, their compassionate heart will grow ever greater. Not only should killing be refrained from; the crawling and moving creatures that contain a spirit are all living lives. To seek silk one boils the cocoons, to hoe the ground one kills insects. When one considers where clothing and food come from, one sees that all of it kills other beings so that one may live; therefore the offense of reckless waste and destruction should rank with the killing of living things. As for the injuries done by one's own hands by mistake and the trampling done by one's own feet by mistake, they are beyond counting, and one should guard against them in every careful way. An old poem says: To love the mice, keep a little rice always by; to pity the moth, do not light the lamp. How benevolent is that. Good deeds are without limit and cannot be recounted to the end. If one can extend the ten matters above, then the ten thousand virtues can be complete.

Compassion is the root of the ten thousand good deeds; it is the very heart of benevolence. Compassion has two meanings: one is to relieve the poor and rescue the suffering, and one is to refrain from killing and to set living things free. Weighing the word itself, it should be understood as reaching out to other beings. It means that the gentleman who piles up virtue and accumulates merit does not stop at loving his kin and being kind to the people; where his compassionate heart reaches, it will extend to other beings as well.

The Great Treasury Sutra says: One who does not kill living beings, who cherishes their lives, and who sets them free and gives them food, obtains the reward of long life. In these days, when children of the household play stubbornly, they should be strictly forbidden to harm or injure any flies or butterflies, insects or ants, birds or sparrows, and the like. It is not only that lives are hurt; it also inflames the killing mind, and when they grow up they will not know benevolence and forbearance. As for servants who pour scalding water, or burn firewood, or sweep the ground, leeches and ants and the like are often hurt by them, and this too should be guarded against. Whenever a person sees any living being cast into a place of death, such as a moth flying into the lamp, an insect falling into a net, a bird or sparrow being wounded, an ant being trodden upon, or fine-scaled fish and shrimp being netted, he should find a skillful way to rescue and save them and keep them whole. This is what those of blessing and long life do.

The Guanshiyin Sutra says: The Great Brahma Heaven King asked what the outward mark of a dharani is, and the bodhisattva answered: the mind of great compassion is its mark. The Huayan Helun says: Guanshiyin represents the western quarter; because the west is the region of autumn and killing, and he practices compassion and rescues the suffering in that very place of killing, he is named Guanshiyin, the Perceiver of the Sounds of the World. The Chapter on Samantabhadra's Vows says: If you make sentient beings happy, then all the Tathagatas are happy. Why is this so? Because all Buddhas and Tathagatas take the mind of great compassion as their substance. It is on account of sentient beings that great compassion arises; on account of great compassion the mind of enlightenment arises; and on account of the mind of enlightenment one accomplishes supreme perfect enlightenment. What sentient beings love most is their body and life; what the Buddhas love most is sentient beings. If one can save the bodies and lives of sentient beings, one can fulfill the vows of all the Buddhas. From this we see that the many words of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas are nothing but teaching people to save sentient beings from suffering, while the many words of demons and outside paths are nothing but teaching people to eat the flesh of sentient beings. Therefore we know that urging people to release life opens the heart of compassion in them and becomes the good cause of long-lasting joy through kalpas without end, while urging people to kill opens the heart of cruelty in them and becomes the root of grievance and offense through kalpas without end. A single word is the pivot of calamity and fortune in this way. Can one fail to be cautious?

In the Han dynasty, Yang Bao, when he was nine years old, saw a yellow sparrow struck down by an owl and fallen to the ground, and then caught fast by ants. Bao rescued it, put it in a box, and fed it on yellow flowers. When its feathers were fully grown he let it go. One evening a boy in yellow robes bowed to Bao and said: I am an envoy of the Queen Mother of the West; I was on my way to Penglai and met with mishap here, and I was moved by your rescue. He then gave him four jade rings and said: May your sons and grandsons hold the three highest offices, and be as spotless as these rings. Having said this he vanished. Later Bao begot Zhen, Zhen begot Bing, Bing begot Ci, and Ci begot Biao; for four generations they held the three highest offices, and their purity was without equal.

In the Ming dynasty, Shen Wansan saw a man holding several hundred frogs and about to kill them, so he bought them all and released them into a pond. One day, passing by the pond, he saw a crowd of frogs squatting in a ring around an earthenware basin. Wansan took it home and used it as a washbasin. Once, when washing his hands, he left a ring in it; the next morning he noticed and went to take it out, and the basin was full of rings. Shen was astonished, and when he tested it with silver and gold the same thing happened: it was a treasure-gathering basin. His wealth rivaled a nation's.

Chan Master Yanshou of the Song dynasty was a man of Danyang. He was at first a clerk of Yuyao county, and fell short of the public money in the treasury by several hundred thousand. The authorities interrogated him, and it turned out that the money had been spent only on buying things to release living creatures; he had not expected such a loss. His crime deserved death, yet as he faced execution his expression did not change. He said: I have released countless living beings alive; now though I die, I go straight to the West. Is this not a joy? The king of Wuyue heard of it and pitied him; he pardoned his crime and let him become a monk. He dreamed that Guanyin poured sweet dew into his mouth, and the clarity of his wisdom opened day by day. He composed the Wan Shan Tong Gui Ji in six fascicles and dwelt at Yongming Monastery, where at the age of ninety-eight he joined his palms and passed away sitting upright; a stupa was raised beside the monastery. A monk walked around that stupa in worship every day, and when people asked him why, he answered: I am a monk of Fuzhou. When I fell ill I went to the underworld, and there I saw a scroll portrait in the corner of the hall, before which King Yama himself was bowing. I asked the presiding clerk, and he answered: This is Chan Master Yanshou. All who die must pass through this place, but this Chan Master went straight to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and was born in the highest grade of the highest rebirth, and so the king reveres and salutes him. Thus it is clear that one who cherishes life goes straight to the West and is honored by the underworld in this way.

Master Lianchi of the Ming dynasty wrote in his Essay on Abstaining from Killing: Every person loves his life, and every creature craves to live. How can you kill another's body to fill your own mouth and belly? Sometimes you split the belly with a sharp blade, sometimes pierce the heart with a pointed knife, sometimes strip the skin and scrape off the scales, sometimes cut the throat and split the shell; sometimes you boil a turtle or an eel alive in scalding water, sometimes you pickle crab and shrimp raw in salt and wine. Pitiful is their great agony with no way to cry out, their extreme suffering beyond endurance. To create such offense as fills the heavens, and to bind up deep enmity for ten thousand generations: in one day of impermanence you fall straight into hell, into cauldrons of boiling water and pits of glowing coals, into sword trees and knife mountains. When your offense there is finished, you are still made a beast, and grievance answers grievance, life repays life. When that repayment is done and you are a human again, you are sickly and die young. I now grieve and warn the people of the world, and universally urge them to abstain from killing. If you can further release living creatures according to your means, and recite the Buddha's name with dedication, you will not only increase your merit and blessing but will surely be born in the Pure Land just as you vow, forever freed from the round of rebirth. The merit is immeasurable.

To be loyal as a minister and filial as a son is the constant of heavenly principle and the root of human relationships. If a minister is not loyal, what can the ruler still hope for from him? If a son is not filial, what can the father still hope for from him? Such a one is not even the equal of the birds and beasts. How can he be called a human being?

Though a person is destined to ascend to the ranks of the immortals, he must pass through many years and long ages. But one who is perfectly loyal and perfectly filial leaves the world today and is born into the heavens tomorrow. People know that loyalty and filial piety are the great duties of minister and son, but how do they not know that they are above all the very root of deliverance?

One who is filial must first bring peace to the state. Bringing peace to the state is the way to bring peace to the family, and bringing peace to the family is the way to practice filial piety. Therefore the ancients sought loyal ministers at the gates of filial sons. Only when loyalty and filial piety are both complete is there the highest virtue and the essential Way. Yet there are also cases in which loyalty and filial piety cannot both be fulfilled to the uttermost; so I set them apart and discuss them, that people may know, according to the matter at hand, where to devote their hearts.

Loyalty means exhausting one's heart without deceit. A person should have it wherever human relationships are found: in serving a superior, in befriending one's peers, in handling affairs and meeting people. Here, however, it is spoken of as belonging specifically to the minister. Between father and son, brothers, and husband and wife, everyone knows by himself to love and respect. But ruler and minister are joined by righteousness, and everyone is apt to be careless and half-hearted there. To speak of loyalty in this connection is what is called the unchanging principle of Heaven and the righteous order of earth, from which there is no escape anywhere between heaven and earth.

Pan Zhongmou said: After the gift of life and of father and mother, the greatest grace a person receives in this world is the ruler's. It makes no difference: in ordinary times he treads the soil and eats its produce, and all of it is imperial grace. He is trained in the schools and academies, and in time becomes an official and receives rank, honor reaching his ancestors and glory extending to the three branches of his clan; perhaps he is treated as a trusted intimate, or raised up to be a shepherd of the people. All of this is meant only to obtain from him the repayment of one who is fostered as a scholar. A person is not grass or a tree; who would not be moved in his heart? Yet one who has personally received the grace of the state never thinks of repaying it as a dog or horse repays its master, but knows only to look after his own person and household. Ask his conscience: how can he bear it?

Yu Tieqiao said: Scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants never see with their own eyes the palace gates of the ninefold court, and so it seems that no ruler's grace can be spoken of in their case. Yet consider a single region: let bandits seize and occupy it, let outlaws rise in arms, and then lust, slaughter, plunder, and seizure leave men not knowing whether they will survive till evening. Had the court's troops and armor, its power to punish and to bless, not destroyed those men and made them safe, how could the whole realm sit and enjoy the blessings of Great Peace? Think of this, and then for the bearer of burdens and the herd boy, for the weaving woman and the plowing man, there is the ruler's grace in every place and the emperor's power in every hour. Each should do his utmost in loyalty according to his station. How much more so for one who reads books and eats the ruler's salary and yet does not know the single word loyalty. That is truly a shame.

The way of a minister is not one. As a chief councillor, loyalty means rectifying the ruler's heart and assisting his government. As a remonstrating official, loyalty means admonishing frankly and correcting what is wrong. As a judicial official, loyalty means upholding the law with fairness and forbearance. As a local administrator, loyalty means loving the people and being diligent in office. As a military officer, loyalty means exerting one's strength and quelling disorder. When one recommends men and holds the literary authority, loyalty means obtaining the right men for the state. The cases are too many to list one by one. Now the things that divide a minister's attention and make him give no thought to ruler or father are several: his person and household, rank and position, power and influence, grudges and favors, and reputation. The thought of person and household, and of rank and position, arises in ordinary men, and the harm it does is still small. The thought of power and influence mostly arises in treacherous men; it often bears on the welfare of the whole realm and state, and the harm in the end falls on the treacherous man himself. As for grudges and favors, and reputation, even those whom the world calls noble men may sometimes not escape them; the calamity of factions from Tang and Song times is exactly this. Only loyalty exhausts the heart without deceit, and where there is no deceit there is perfect sincerity. With perfect sincerity, every movement of the mind and every thought is wholly free of regard for one's own person, household, rank, or position. One does not shrink before the powerful, does not bend to please personal ties, does not grudge fame and merit, and does not even seek the reputation of loyalty and uprightness. One may bend a little to get a thing done without flattering or toadying; one may uphold the law without turning aside, and yet without angry extremism. One asks only that the measure truly benefit the state's plans and the people's livelihood, and one regards one's ruler truly as a Yao or a Shun among rulers, never daring to harbor a thought of contempt. Only this is loyal reverence.

The Outer Commentary to the Han Book of Songs says: There are three ways of loyalty. To cover the ruler with the Way and serve him so is called great loyalty. To harmonize the ruler with virtue and support him so is called the next loyalty. To use what is right to remonstrate against what is wrong and so rescue him is called lesser loyalty. The Garden of Persuasions says: To follow a command that benefits the ruler is compliance. To follow a command that harms the ruler is flattery. To oppose a command that harms the ruler is rebellion. To oppose a command that benefits the ruler is loyalty.

Yan Guangzhong said: Whenever a man holds office and deals with the affairs of the age, the places of great right and wrong and great benefit and harm often involve his very life. In leisure he may be able to order affairs and hold fast to what is right, but when he comes to such a place he stammers and will not step forward, wavering to save his own neck. Then there are those who kill others to flatter others; and if not, there are those who hedge and dodge like a rat, ruining the state's affairs, so that the world suffers their disorder. From ancient times the heroes who undertook great matters and achieved great merit and a great character all came out of a thousand deaths and one life. Only if a man gains a settled power within himself does the state at last get use of him. Such were Lord Zhuge's bending his strength to the utmost till death, Duke Guo's riding alone to face the invaders, Li Linhuai's placing his knife in his boot, Prince Han of Qi's having four fingers left of ten, and Liu Shunchang's piling firewood to await the end. They moved in and out among ten thousand soldiers with arrows and stones falling thick, and their spirit never stirred; silently they won the victory. How easy was that? They had long since given their bodies over to the state as its own. Yet these, one may say, were fighting generals. As for Xu Yougong, Duke Di of Liang, and Li Fan, all of whom fell under sentence of death, and Duke Pei of Jin, Duke Zhang of Wei, and Duke Han of Wei, who entrusted their lives to swordsmen and assassins, in the end they did not die, and their merit filled heaven and earth and their names hung with the sun and moon. They were able to let go so completely, and therefore great employment followed them. From this we know that the Creator and the ghosts and spirits also use this to test men. If a man passes the test, the spirits furnish him protection and the universe rests on his support. If he fails the test, both his person and his name are ruined. Such were Wang Yan and Yin Hao and others of that kind. At the beginning they too thought themselves standing sheer as a wall ten thousand fathoms high, their renown blazing through the four seas; but they rejoiced at the sight of grass and trembled at the sight of a wolf, for the substance of a sheep was still in them. Once an upheaval came, they croaked and clacked their tongues. How could such men contend for the fate of heaven and earth and settle the nature of men and things? The root they had planted was false from the first. Falsehood pays back falsehood; perhaps they received some small blessing and fortune, and already counted it a gain. But alas, they enjoyed too great a name and thought too highly of themselves; and when the time came for them to drag their feet and show their hands, not a single plan could they unfold, and they became the laughingstock of the world. Speaking from this, the spirits observe what is hidden in a man, and it is not permitted to deceive Heaven or delude men and trust to luck for success. Therefore in this place one must urgently sweep oneself clean. Give this body over to heaven and earth and the ten thousand things; and even if one dies in misfortune, what of it? The deaths of Guan Zhuangmu, Zhang Suiyang, Yue Wumu, and Wen Wenshan, compared with those of Li Linfu, Yang Guozhong, Han Tuozhou, and Jia Sidao, how do they stand? Who among men does not die? But only the upright, the loyal, and the filial become spirits in death. The court grants them conspicuous posthumous honors, their worship is splendid and bright, their descendants eat the shade of their favor. Never has one seen the death of a powerful traitor come to this. Not to speak of the powerful traitors: men like Geshu Han, Xiao Zhizhong, Wang Ya, and Jia Su, who fawned and clung in feebleness to preserve their own necks, yet when their final limit arrived were destroyed root and branch with no remnant. Had they known earlier that they would die a violent death like this in any case, why did they not go forth blazing and magnificent, standing with their heads against heaven and their feet on the earth? Again, in the times of Emperor Wu of Han and Empress Wu of Tang, what a state the world was in. Those who were destroyed in those days without cause were beyond counting, and yet among the officials who upheld fairness at that time, not one died. Those who fawned on the ruler's will and were cruel and vicious never failed to die. Even if one may not judge calamity and fortune entirely by this, is it not all the more reason to trust in the mandate that governs life? Why then be anxious and fearful, begrudging one's own life and breath, betraying the ruler's grace and planting poison in the world?

In the time of Emperor Dezong of Tang, Li Bi was chief councillor. Because of the Grand Princess of Gao, Dezong wished to depose the crown prince, and he summoned Li Bi and told him so, adding that Prince Shu had lately grown up, and was filial, friendly, gentle, and kind. Li Bi said: Your Majesty has only one son; why would you depose him and set up a nephew? Moreover, if you are already suspicious of the son born of your own body, what will you have for a nephew? Though Prince Shu is filial now, from today on Your Majesty should strive, and no longer hope for his filial piety. The emperor said: Do you not love your clan and family? He replied: It is precisely because I love my clan and family that I dare not fail to speak my whole mind. If I feared Your Majesty's great wrath and bent to obey, then tomorrow when Your Majesty repented of it, you would surely blame me, saying: I entrusted you alone with the chancellorship, and you did not remonstrate with all your strength, and so it came to this; and you would surely put my sons to death as well. I am old, and my remaining years are not worth begrudging. But if my sons were wrongfully killed and I were made to take a nephew as my heir, I do not know whether I could enjoy their offerings. With this he sobbed and wept. The emperor wept too and said: The matter has already gone this far; what is to be done? Li Bi replied: This is a great matter; I beg Your Majesty to consider it carefully. From ancient times, when father and son have doubted each other, no state has failed to perish. The emperor said: In the eras of Zhenguan and Kaiyuan, both changed crown princes; why did they not perish? He replied: When Chengqian's plot of rebellion was discovered, Taizong had no choice but to depose him, and he deposed Prince Tai of Wei as well. As for Consort Wu of Hui slandering the crown prince Ying and his brothers and having them killed, the whole realm was resentful and angry; that is a warning for a hundred generations, and how can it be taken as a model? I beg Your Majesty to take three days at leisure and trace the matter to its source; you will surely see clearly that the crown prince has done nothing wrong. If he has in fact shown such traces, I beg Your Majesty to follow the law of Zhenguan and depose Prince Shu as well, and then set up the imperial grandson; then after a hundred generations, the one who holds the realm will still be Your Majesty's own descendant. Had men like Yang Su, Xu Jingzong, and Li Linfu received such a decree, they would already have gone to Prince Shu and plotted to secure the merit of establishing a new ruler. The emperor said: I will put it off for you and think it over tomorrow. Li Bi said: If so, then I know that Your Majesty, father and son, are kind and filial as at the first. But Your Majesty must consider it privately, and not let this thought show to those around you; if it shows, they will all want to establish merit with Prince Shu, and the crown prince will be in danger. A day later the emperor opened the Yanying Hall and summoned Li Bi alone, and said with tears: Had you not spoken so urgently, my repentance today would have come too late. The crown prince is kind and filial, and in truth there is nothing else. Li Bi served four reigns and was a famous chief councillor of Tang; in the end he became an immortal.

In the Tang dynasty Wei Zheng had courage and strategy, and was good at turning the emperor's mind around. Whatever the matter, great or small, he always remonstrated frankly even at the risk of offending, and even when the emperor was extremely angry he did not stop. The emperor once obtained a fine sparrow hawk and carried it on his own arm, and when he saw Zheng coming he hid it in his bosom. Zheng reported on affairs at length on purpose, and the hawk died in his bosom. When Empress Wende passed away, the emperor's thoughts of her never ceased, and he built a storied tower in the park from which to look toward Zhaoling. Once he brought Zheng up with him and made him look. Zheng peered carefully and said: My eyes are dim and I cannot see it. The emperor pointed it out to him. Zheng said: I thought Your Majesty was looking toward Xianling; if it were Zhaoling, then I would of course have seen it long ago. The emperor wept, and for this destroyed the tower. Zheng urged the emperor to lay aside arms and cultivate the civil arts, saying that once the central realm was at peace, the four barbarian peoples would submit of themselves. The emperor followed his words, and afterwards Jiali was taken captive, his chieftains all bore swords as palace guards, and outer doors were left unbolted while travelers carried no provisions. All this was Zheng's doing. Zheng was a famous minister of Tang and was the first to be enfeoffed as Duke of Zheng; his fifth-generation descendant Mo became chief councillor in his turn.

In the time of Empress Wu Zetian, the judicial officials vied in cruelty, and the assistant director of punishments Xu Yougong alone kept to fairness and forbearance. He had first been judicial officer of Puzhou, where he never used the rods to beat anyone. The clerks made a pact among themselves: whoever is punished with the rod by Judicial Officer Xu, we will all together denounce. When his term of office was full he had not beaten a single man, and yet the business of his office was well ordered. When he became assistant director of punishments, all those falsely accused and framed by the cruel officials were vindicated by him, and those he saved from death were beyond counting. He once argued a case before the court, and the empress questioned him with a stern face, but Yougong's expression did not falter and he argued all the more earnestly. Though the empress loved killing, she knew that Yougong was upright and greatly respected and feared him. Zhou Xing and the others slandered and reviled him in a hundred ways, and in the end could not harm him. He was afterwards promoted to attendant censor of the left of the palace court, and his sons and grandsons were repeatedly prominent.

In the Tang dynasty Guo Ziyi, during the Anshi rebellion, recovered the two capitals and his merit surpassed that of all the other generals. In the time of Emperor Daizong, when the eunuchs held power, Ziyi was left idle and out of office for a long time and his troops scattered; then the Tibetans suddenly invaded, the capital was shaken with terror, and the emperor fled to Shanzhou. Great generals such as Li Guangbi all resented the eunuchs' power and held their troops back without coming. Ziyi alone, having gathered twenty horsemen by recruitment, set out at once. He assembled the various generals, beat the drums, spread the banners, and lit many fires to make the Tibetans suspect a great host. The Tibetans were frightened and all their host fled away. Afterwards they came again with the Uighurs, a multitude of several hundred thousand, and the various generals for the most part did not arrive in time. Ziyi went alone on a single horse to persuade the Uighurs, and utterly defeated the Tibetans. Though Ziyi was a great general commanding strong troops, and though Cheng Yuanzhen and Yu Chaoen slandered and reviled him in a hundred ways, one sheet of an imperial decree summoning him never failed to find him on the road the same day; and so slander and defamation could not take hold. He held the office of director of the secretariat for a full twenty-four terms of assessment, was enfeoffed as Prince of Fenyang, and had eight sons and seven sons-in-law; no one could match his prominence and prosperity.

In the Song dynasty Sima Wengong, as chief councillor, gave his body to the state and labored diligently over the manifold affairs of government. He was already ill at the time, and yet the laws of the green sprouts loans, the service exemption, and the military officers still stood, and the Western Xia had not submitted. He sighed and said: With these four harms unremoved, I shall die with my eyes unclosed. When guests saw how thin he had grown, they brought up Zhuge Liang, who ate little while his affairs were many, as a warning. The duke said: Life and death are the mandate of Heaven. He labored all the harder at it. When his illness became critical he was no longer conscious of himself, yet he murmured earnestly as if speaking in a dream, and it was all of the court and the affairs of the realm.

Emperor Gaozong of Wei said to his assembled ministers: A ruler and a father are one and the same. When a father has a fault, a son who does not memorialize about it in front of the crowd but remonstrates in a private room apart does so because he does not wish to make his father's evil known. Men like Gao Yun: whenever I had a fault, he never failed to speak of it to my face, even to the point of saying what I could not bear to hear. I knew my fault, and yet the world did not know it. Can this not be called loyalty? The single-hearted loyalty of Gao Yun is something not only the passionate cannot achieve, but also something the subtly persuasive cannot reach. It may serve as a model of remonstrance.

In the Song dynasty Su Bing submitted a memorial discussing affairs of state and was banished to Raozhou. Passing through Luo, he lodged with Yin Tun and was rather preoccupied with his demotion. Yin Tun said: When you submitted your memorial, were you planning for the state, or planning for yourself? If you were planning for the state, you should go to Raozhou gladly. If you were planning for advancement, then banishment to Raozhou is still a light sentence. At this Su Bing was suddenly clear and untroubled. Zhang Kean said: For a scholar in office, if there is in him a heart that clings to merit and fame and seeks to please and be liked, then he will accomplish not one thing. How true those words are.

Looking over all ages, ministers who exhausted their loyalty and received their reward are too many to recount. As for those who would not yield in the great issues and gave their lives when they saw danger, their lot was often hard and they carried their regret for a thousand years, so that it seems Heaven's recompense was strangely otherwise in their case. But they did not know that in life they enjoyed the highest renown of their age, and in death they receive the bowing and kneeling of ten thousand people; Heaven's recompense to them is more than a hundredfold that of those who enjoy wealth, honor, ease, and pleasure in their own persons. And the misery of Heaven's recompense for those who forget their ruler and injure the people need not even be spoken of. For now let us not discuss the retribution of loyalty or the lack of it. Look only at those who drift vaguely along, whose minds are not set on the common people: they too have no good ending. From this we see that these salaries and emoluments of yours can certainly not be enjoyed while betraying this single word. From chief councillor down to the common people, there are many duties of loyalty that should be fulfilled. But the lives of the common folk are most bound up with the county magistrate, and so the magistrate above all must not be disloyal. The state establishes this magistracy and requires it to nourish the people. The ancients said: The people are the foundation of the state, and when the foundation is firm the state is at peace. With so heavy a charge entrusted to him, how can he be permitted to betray it? Thus when a man studies, he should truly and earnestly arouse the mind that saves the world; and when he holds power and rides on circumstances, he must keep Heaven and earth, ruler and parents constantly in mind, widely perform good deeds, be pure and cautious in leading his subordinates, diligently inquire into the people's hidden hardships, imitate the excellent government of the Cheng brothers and Zhu Xi, and ask the worthy men of the day for good models. Do not bend to personal ties; do not covet wealth. Honor the good and punish the violent; promote what benefits and remove what harms. Advocate the community compact; value farming and sericulture. Instruct the scholars in the study of principle; teach the people diligence and thrift. In pressing for taxes, always think of good methods; in cases of punishment, always exhaust your humane heart. Reform the cunning ways; watch out for wicked clerks. In flood and drought, investigate early and report quickly; in famine, find means of relief. For widowers, widows, orphans, and the childless, see that there is someone charged with their support. For dikes, banks, ditches, and canals, encourage repair and see that it is effective. Strictly forbid such evils as drowning infant girls, seizure and sale of persons, gambling, brothels, spirit processions, theatrical shows, obscene books, exposure of coffins, and slaughter of cattle. Promote such good works as community granaries, the Society of Shared Goodness, foundling homes, free schools, public burial grounds, summer medicine dispensaries, winter gruel stations, printing offices, and shelters for the wandering. Do so as though gathering treasures from a mountain of jewels. In the commentary above it has already been said that a local administrator's loyalty lies in loving the people and being diligent in office; and now I do not shrink from speaking again and again with a bitter mouth, because this truly is what most concerns the people's lives. If one can hold to a single thought of this, what matter will not be accomplished? How can his merit and blessing be measured? I further append several cases especially, as observation and encouragement for those who are fathers and mothers to the people.

In the Song dynasty Cheng Mingdao, as magistrate of Jincheng, rectified himself and led others by example, teaching the people by ritual and righteousness. Whenever a person came to the town on business, he would always tell him of filial piety, fraternal duty, loyalty, and good faith, of how at home to serve father and elder brother and abroad to serve elders and superiors. He measured the distance of the villages and formed them into mutual-aid groups, so that they helped one another in labor service and relieved one another in hardship and calamity, and the cunning and false could find no place among them. All who were orphaned, solitary, crippled, or disabled he charged to their relatives and neighbors, so that none should lose his place in the world. Travelers on the road who fell ill were all cared for. He accordingly established village schools, more than sixty of them. In his leisure he went in person, called the elders together, and talked with them, inquiring into the people's sufferings. In the books the children studied, he himself marked the punctuation and phrasing; and if a teacher was not good, he had him replaced. He selected the outstanding pupils, gathered them, and taught them. He joined the villagers into societies, set up rules and articles, and distinguished good from evil, so that they had encouragement and a sense of shame. Mingdao looked on the people as his own children. Those who had business to conduct might come straight to the court below without a written petition and state their case there; the master would speak to them calmly and instruct them earnestly without ever wearying. During three years in the town the people loved him as a father and mother, and on the day he left, the sound of weeping shook the countryside. In the region where Mingdao faced government, high and low alike were stirred. It was because he had what harmonized the feelings of the multitude, and so they were stirred; the creative working of heaven and earth is simply this stirring.

While Mingdao was acting as magistrate of the town, in midsummer the pond embankment broke in a great flood. By law the matter had to be reported to the prefecture, and the prefecture had to report it to the grain transport office, so that more than a month would pass before work could begin. The master feared the seedlings would wither, and said: To save the people, I will not decline to be punished for it. He then called out the people and closed the breach. That year there was a great harvest.

As registrar of Shangyuan in the Hedong circuit, where the revenues were insufficient, whenever the government made requisitions the prices soared and every year this became a scourge for the people. The master estimated what was required and had the rich households fix in advance the price at which they would store it and put it out, so that the rich households did not lose their profit while the people's expense was no more than two or three tenths of what it had been. Again, the people's tax grain was habitually transported to the nearby frontier; carried there, the road was long, and bought locally, the price was high. The master chose those among the rich whom he could trust and had them buy up grain in advance in the frontier commandery, so that the expense was greatly reduced and the people's strength was eased.

As magistrate of Fugou, there were people who burned and plundered the boats and property of boatmen, and it happened more than a dozen times every year. The master caught one man and made him name his fellows, and so obtained several dozen. He did not prosecute them further for their old offenses, but settled them in separate districts, made them take up the trade of towing boats, and had them keep watch for those who did evil. From this time the region had no more trouble with burned boats.

While governing a county of the capital region, there was a flood and the people were starving. The master asked to open the grain stores and lend grain to them. The director of agriculture was angry and sent an inspector to verify the facts; the envoy reported that no loan should be made. The master begged for the loan without ceasing, and at last obtained six thousand piculs of grain, and the starving were relieved. The director of agriculture grew angrier still, and seeing in the loan registers that households of the same grade had received loans of different amounts, he sent a directive that the county should flog the responsible clerk. The master said: Relieving famine should be according to the number of mouths, not according to the grade of the household; moreover it was the magistrate himself who did it, and it is no fault of the clerk. So the matter was dropped. The master once said: The duty of a magistrate is to ensure that within his borders, in bad years and years of famine, the people escape death, eat their fill, and live at ease, and have the instruction of ritual and righteousness. Only then is the office fulfilled.

As magistrate of Fugou he led the people to open and dredge the ditches and channels with all their strength. It is a pity he could not finish the work, for he was transferred elsewhere and it came to a stop. The master once supervised the labor himself, and though the cold was bitter or the sun blazing he neither wore a fur coat nor held a canopy. When he made his rounds no one could tell where he would arrive, and so each man did his utmost of himself, and they often finished the work ahead of time. Wherever the master served as a county official, he wrote at his seat the four words, look on the people as wounded. He often said: I am always ashamed before those four words.

In the Song dynasty, when Master Zhu Xi was magistrate of Zhangzhou, he said: I wish to give attention to the schools. I asked Huang Zhilu to be a model for the students, and I have also invited senior scholars to be models together with him, so that the young scholars may know something of which way to face, and know the method of doing good, and so that together with the people of this whole region they may move toward the realm of the noble. And because the customs did not yet know ritual, he selected the ancient rites of burial, mourning, marriage, and taking a wife and posted them up to show the people, and had the elders explain them so as to teach the young. He forbade the people of Zhangzhou the assemblies and the pilgrimages to the sacred peak, saying: If it does nothing but confuse men and women together, then it should be prohibited. He also abolished the unnamed levies of the subordinate counties, remitting seven million a year. He once went to Tangshi, where he received old peasants and woodcutters as if welcoming honored guests, with not the least hedge or boundary between them, saying: If people of this sort are cut off from me by the distance of rank, how will they be able to tell me their true feelings?

The proclamation as magistrate of Nankang: This commandery has poor soil and few people, its labor services are vexatious and its taxes heavy, and the strength of the people grows more straitened by the day. This is deeply pitiable. Hereafter, if among the scholars, elders, monks, and Daoists within my jurisdiction, and among the soldiers and civilians of every kind and description, there are any who know the root of these ills and benefits, and how in due order they should be dealt with and what should be done to give relief, let them all set it out in careful detail with the actual facts, and at any hour of day or night come and lay it before the commandery. I will await them and question them face to face, and take measures in every way I can, so that the population may increase year by year and every household have enough.

His exhortation as magistrate of Nankang: Tenant farmers who till the fields of a landlord put forth the greater part of the labor, and they depend entirely on the landlord to lend and supply them, to treat them with kindness and give them relief, and not to let them lose their place.

His exhortation to official households: Since you are called a family of officials, you are different from ordinary people, and you should all the more keep to your station and follow principle, and strive to restrain yourselves and benefit others.

His exhortation concerning the mutual admonition of the mutual-aid groups: Let the members of each group admonish one another. Be filial to father and mother, respectful to elders and superiors, harmonious with kin by blood and by marriage, and generous in relieving your neighbors. Let each keep to his own station and attend to his own calling. Do not commit villainy or theft; do not give way to drink or gambling; do not fight or strike one another; do not go to law against one another. Where there are filial sons and obedient grandsons, righteous husbands and chaste wives whose deeds are conspicuous, report them at once, and they shall be honored and rewarded according to the regulations. Those who do not follow this teaching, report and denounce them likewise, and they shall be investigated and dealt with according to law.

As magistrate of Nankang, every five days he went to the school and received the students, and earnestly expounded the teaching for all. He said: I now feel rather that there is a stirring among them. Give it a little more than a month, and there should be some change from the crudeness of before.

As an official at Chong'an, because the people were starving he petitioned the prefect, Lord Xu Jia, and obtained six hundred piculs of rice to lend to them, and on that basis established a community granary. Thirty years later it had accumulated a hundred thousand piculs, which were distributed in years of poor harvest, and so the district had no more years of famine.
